# PATTERN 6: Spatial Index Pattern
# ============================================================================
print("\n" + "=" * 80)
print("6. SPATIAL INDEX PATTERN")
print("-" * 80)
print("""
Purpose: Optimize queries on geographic/spatial data
Strategy: Use geohashing, grid partitioning, and spatial bucketing
""")

class SpatialIndexPattern:
    """
    Implements spatial indexing for geographic data using geohashing
    and grid-based partitioning. Useful for location-based queries.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def create_location_data(self):
        """Create sample location data (stores, delivery points, etc.)"""
        data = [
            (1, "Store A", 40.7128, -74.0060, "New York", "USA"),      # New York
            (2, "Store B", 40.7580, -73.9855, "New York", "USA"),      # Times Square
            (3, "Store C", 34.0522, -118.2437, "Los Angeles", "USA"),  # LA
            (4, "Store D", 51.5074, -0.1278, "London", "UK"),          # London
            (5, "Store E", 48.8566, 2.3522, "Paris", "France"),        # Paris
            (6, "Store F", 35.6762, 139.6503, "Tokyo", "Japan"),       # Tokyo
            (7, "Store G", 40.7489, -73.9680, "New York", "USA"),      # Near Times Square
            (8, "Store H", 34.0195, -118.4912, "Los Angeles", "USA"),  # Santa Monica
            (9, "Store I", 51.5155, -0.0922, "London", "UK"),          # East London
            (10, "Store J", 48.8738, 2.2950, "Paris", "France")        # West Paris
        ]
        
        schema = StructType([
            StructField("store_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("store_name", StringType(), False),
            StructField("latitude", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("longitude", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("city", StringType(), False),
            StructField("country", StringType(), False)
        ])
        
        return self.spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    def geohash_encode(self, lat, lon, precision=6):
        """
        Simple geohash encoding function
        Note: For production, use a proper geohash library
        """
        from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
        from pyspark.sql.types import StringType
        
        def encode_geohash(latitude, longitude):
            """Basic geohash encoding implementation"""
            if latitude is None or longitude is None:
                return None
            
            # Simple grid-based geohash for demonstration
            # In production, use proper geohash libraries like python-geohash
            lat_grid = int((latitude + 90) * 100)
            lon_grid = int((longitude + 180) * 100)
            
            return f"{lat_grid:05d}_{lon_grid:05d}"
        
        return udf(encode_geohash, StringType())
    
    def create_geohash_index(self, df, output_path):
        """
        Create spatial index using geohash
        Groups nearby locations together for efficient proximity queries
        """
        print("\nCreating spatial index using geohash...")
        
        # Add geohash column
        geohash_udf = self.geohash_encode()
        indexed_df = df.withColumn("geohash", geohash_udf(col("latitude"), col("longitude")))
        
        # Add grid coordinates for partitioning
        indexed_df = indexed_df \
            .withColumn("lat_grid", ((col("latitude") + 90) * 10).cast("int")) \
            .withColumn("lon_grid", ((col("longitude") + 180) * 10).cast("int"))
        
        # Partition by geohash for spatial locality
        indexed_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("country", "lat_grid") \
            .parquet(output_path)
        
        print(f"Geohash spatial index created at: {output_path}")
        
        result_df = self.spark.read.parquet(output_path)
        result_df.cache()
        
        return result_df
    
    def create_grid_based_index(self, df, grid_size, output_path):
        """
        Create spatial index using grid partitioning
        Divides the world into grid cells
        """
        print(f"\nCreating grid-based spatial index (grid size: {grid_size})...")
        
        # Create grid cells
        indexed_df = df \
            .withColumn("grid_lat", (col("latitude") / grid_size).cast("int")) \
            .withColumn("grid_lon", (col("longitude") / grid_size).cast("int")) \
            .withColumn("grid_cell", 
                       concat(col("grid_lat").cast("string"), 
                              lit("_"), 
                              col("grid_lon").cast("string")))
        
        # Partition by grid cell
        indexed_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("grid_cell") \
            .parquet(output_path)
        
        print(f"Grid-based spatial index created at: {output_path}")
        
        result_df = self.spark.read.parquet(output_path)
        result_df.cache()
        
        return result_df
    
    def calculate_distance(self):
        """
        UDF to calculate Haversine distance between two points
        Returns distance in kilometers
        """
        from pyspark.sql.functions import udf
        from pyspark.sql.types import DoubleType
        import math
        
        def haversine_distance(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2):
            """Calculate distance using Haversine formula"""
            if None in [lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2]:
                return None
            
            # Convert to radians
            lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2 = map(math.radians, [lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2])
            
            # Haversine formula
            dlat = lat2 - lat1
            dlon = lon2 - lon1
            a = math.sin(dlat/2)**2 + math.cos(lat1) * math.cos(lat2) * math.sin(dlon/2)**2
            c = 2 * math.asin(math.sqrt(a))
            
            # Earth radius in kilometers
            r = 6371
            
            return c * r
        
        return udf(haversine_distance, DoubleType())
    
    def create_proximity_index(self, df, reference_points, output_path):
        """
        Create index based on proximity to reference points
        Useful for nearest store/facility queries
        """
        print("\nCreating proximity-based spatial index...")
        
        distance_udf = self.calculate_distance()
        
        # Calculate distance to each reference point
        indexed_df = df
        
        for idx, (ref_name, ref_lat, ref_lon) in enumerate(reference_points):
            indexed_df = indexed_df.withColumn(
                f"dist_to_{ref_name}",
                distance_udf(col("latitude"), col("longitude"), 
                           lit(ref_lat), lit(ref_lon))
            )
        
        # Add nearest reference point
        distance_cols = [f"dist_to_{name}" for name, _, _ in reference_points]
        
        # Find minimum distance and corresponding reference point
        indexed_df = indexed_df.withColumn(
            "nearest_distance",
            least(*[col(dc) for dc in distance_cols])
        )
        
        # Save with partitioning
        indexed_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("country") \
            .parquet(output_path)
        
        print(f"Proximity spatial index created at: {output_path}")
        
        result_df = self.spark.read.parquet(output_path)
        result_df.cache()
        
        return result_df
    
    def demonstrate_spatial_queries(self, geohash_idx, grid_idx, proximity_idx):
        """Demonstrate spatial queries using different index types"""
        
        print("\n--- Query 1: Find stores in same geohash (nearby locations) ---")
        
        # Group by geohash to find co-located stores
        geohash_result = geohash_idx.groupBy("geohash", "city") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("store_count"),
                collect_list("store_name").alias("stores")
            ) \
            .filter(col("store_count") > 1) \
            .orderBy(desc("store_count"))
        
        geohash_result.show(truncate=False)
        
        print("\n--- Query 2: Find stores in specific grid cell ---")
        
        # Query specific grid cell
        grid_result = grid_idx.filter(col("grid_cell") == "13_10") \
            .select("store_name", "city", "latitude", "longitude", "grid_cell")
        
        grid_result.show()
        
        print("\n--- Query 3: Find stores by proximity to reference point ---")
        
        # Find closest stores
        proximity_result = proximity_idx \
            .select("store_name", "city", "nearest_distance") \
            .orderBy("nearest_distance") \
            .limit(5)
        
        proximity_result.show()
        
        print("\n--- Query 4: Stores within bounding box ---")
        
        # Bounding box query (e.g., New York area)
        bbox_result = geohash_idx.filter(
            (col("latitude").between(40.7, 40.8)) &
            (col("longitude").between(-74.1, -73.9))
        ).select("store_name", "city", "latitude", "longitude")
        
        bbox_result.show()
        
        return geohash_result, grid_result, proximity_result, bbox_result

class IndexingBestPractices:
    """
    Demonstrates best practices and performance comparisons for different
    indexing strategies.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def print_index_comparison_table(self):
        """Print comparison table of all indexing patterns"""
        
        comparison_data = [
            ("Single-Column", "High", "Low", "Simple filters", "Partitioning/Bucketing"),
            ("Multi-Column", "Very High", "Medium", "Complex filters", "Hierarchical partitioning"),
            ("Covering", "Very High", "High", "Avoid joins", "Denormalization + Cache"),
            ("Partial", "High", "Low", "Subset queries", "Filtered partitioning"),
            ("Functional", "High", "Medium", "Computed values", "Derived columns + Index"),
            ("Spatial", "Very High", "High", "Geographic queries", "Geohash/Grid partitioning")
        ]
        
        schema = StructType([
            StructField("Pattern", StringType(), False),
            StructField("Query_Speed", StringType(), False),
            StructField("Storage_Cost", StringType(), False),
            StructField("Best_For", StringType(), False),
            StructField("Implementation", StringType(), False)
        ])
        
        comparison_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(comparison_data, schema)
        
        print("\nIndexing Pattern Comparison:")
        comparison_df.show(truncate=False)
        
        return comparison_df
    
    def demonstrate_index_selection_guidelines(self):
        """Provide guidelines for selecting appropriate index pattern"""
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("INDEX SELECTION GUIDELINES")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        guidelines = """
        
1. SINGLE-COLUMN INDEX
   Use When:
   - Queries filter on one column frequently
   - Column has moderate cardinality (10-10,000 unique values)
   - Simple equality or range queries
   
   Example: WHERE department = 'Sales'
   
2. MULTI-COLUMN INDEX
   Use When:
   - Queries filter on multiple columns together
   - Columns have correlation (e.g., country + state)
   - Need hierarchical filtering
   
   Example: WHERE country = 'USA' AND state = 'CA'
   
3. COVERING INDEX
   Use When:
   - Queries need multiple columns from different tables
   - Join operations are expensive
   - Read-heavy workload with specific query patterns
   
   Example: Denormalized view for dashboards
   
4. PARTIAL INDEX
   Use When:
   - Only a subset of data is frequently queried
   - Want to reduce index size and maintenance
   - Have clear data lifecycle (active vs archived)
   
   Example: Index only pending/failed transactions
   
5. FUNCTIONAL INDEX
   Use When:
   - Queries use computed or transformed values
   - Need case-insensitive searches
   - Queries on date parts or mathematical calculations
   
   Example: WHERE UPPER(name) = 'JOHN' or WHERE YEAR(date) = 2023
   
6. SPATIAL INDEX
   Use When:
   - Working with geographic/location data
   - Need proximity or bounding box queries
   - Require nearest-neighbor searches
   
   Example: Find stores within 5km radius
        """
        
        print(guidelines)
    
    def demonstrate_performance_tips(self):
        """Demonstrate performance optimization tips"""
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("PERFORMANCE OPTIMIZATION TIPS")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        tips = """
        
PARTITIONING BEST PRACTICES:
✓ Choose columns with low-to-moderate cardinality (< 10,000 partitions)
✓ Avoid over-partitioning (small files problem)
✓ Use date-based partitioning for time-series data
✓ Partition on most frequently filtered columns
✗ Don't partition on high-cardinality columns (IDs, timestamps)

BUCKETING BEST PRACTICES:
✓ Use for join optimization (same bucketing on both tables)
✓ Choose number of buckets as power of 2 or multiple of cluster size
✓ Bucket on columns used in joins and aggregations
✓ Combine with sorting for better compression
✗ Don't use bucketing with very small datasets

CACHING STRATEGIES:
✓ Cache frequently accessed indexes
✓ Use MEMORY_AND_DISK for large indexes
✓ Unpersist when no longer needed
✓ Monitor cache usage with spark.catalog.isCached()

Z-ORDERING (Delta Lake):
✓ Use for multi-column filtering
✓ Order columns by query frequency
✓ Combine with partitioning for best results
✓ Re-optimize periodically

FILE SIZE OPTIMIZATION:
✓ Target 128MB - 1GB per file
✓ Use coalesce() or repartition() to control file count
✓ Enable adaptive query execution
✓ Use compression (snappy, gzip, zstd)

STATISTICS COLLECTION:
✓ Enable cost-based optimizer (CBO)
✓ Collect column statistics for better query plans
✓ Use ANALYZE TABLE commands
✓ Update statistics after major data changes
        """
        
        print(tips)
    
    def create_performance_benchmark(self):
        """Create a simple performance benchmark example"""
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("PERFORMANCE BENCHMARK EXAMPLE")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # Create larger dataset for benchmarking
        print("\nCreating benchmark dataset (10,000 records)...")
        
        from pyspark.sql.functions import rand, randn
        
        benchmark_df = self.spark.range(0, 10000) \
            .withColumn("category", (rand() * 10).cast("int").cast("string")) \
            .withColumn("region", (rand() * 5).cast("int").cast("string")) \
            .withColumn("value", randn() * 1000) \
            .withColumn("timestamp", 
                       expr("date_sub(current_date(), cast(rand() * 365 as int))"))
        
        print(f"Benchmark dataset created: {benchmark_df.count()} records")
        
        # Scenario 1: No indexing
        print("\n--- Scenario 1: No Indexing ---")
        benchmark_df.write.mode("overwrite").parquet("/tmp/benchmark_no_index")
        no_index_df = self.spark.read.parquet("/tmp/benchmark_no_index")
        
        # Scenario 2: Single-column partitioning
        print("\n--- Scenario 2: Single-Column Partitioning ---")
        benchmark_df.write.mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("category") \
            .parquet("/tmp/benchmark_single_partition")
        single_partition_df = self.spark.read.parquet("/tmp/benchmark_single_partition")
        
        # Scenario 3: Multi-column partitioning
        print("\n--- Scenario 3: Multi-Column Partitioning ---")
        benchmark_df.write.mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("category", "region") \
            .parquet("/tmp/benchmark_multi_partition")
        multi_partition_df = self.spark.read.parquet("/tmp/benchmark_multi_partition")
        
        # Run test query on each scenario
        test_filter = (col("category") == "5") & (col("region") == "2")
        
        print("\n--- Query Performance Comparison ---")
        print("Test Query: Filter on category=5 AND region=2")
        
        # Query 1: No index
        print("\n1. No Indexing:")
        result1 = no_index_df.filter(test_filter).count()
        print(f"   Result count: {result1}")
        no_index_df.filter(test_filter).explain(mode="simple")
        
        # Query 2: Single partition
        print("\n2. Single-Column Partition:")
        result2 = single_partition_df.filter(test_filter).count()
        print(f"   Result count: {result2}")
        single_partition_df.filter(test_filter).explain(mode="simple")
        
        # Query 3: Multi partition
        print("\n3. Multi-Column Partition:")
        result3 = multi_partition_df.filter(test_filter).count()
        print(f"   Result count: {result3}")
        multi_partition_df.filter(test_filter).explain(mode="simple")
        
        return benchmark_df
    
    def demonstrate_index_maintenance(self):
        """Demonstrate index maintenance operations"""
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("INDEX MAINTENANCE OPERATIONS")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        maintenance_guide = """
        
REGULAR MAINTENANCE TASKS:

1. STATISTICS UPDATE:
   spark.sql("ANALYZE TABLE table_name COMPUTE STATISTICS")
   spark.sql("ANALYZE TABLE table_name COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS col1, col2")

2. COMPACT SMALL FILES:
   df.coalesce(num_partitions).write.mode("overwrite").save(path)
   
3. CACHE MANAGEMENT:
   spark.catalog.clearCache()  # Clear all cached tables
   df.unpersist()              # Unpersist specific DataFrame

4. PARTITION PRUNING VERIFICATION:
   df.filter(...).explain(extended=True)  # Check for partition pruning

5. MONITOR INDEX EFFECTIVENESS:
   - Check query execution plans
   - Monitor partition skew
   - Track cache hit rates
   - Analyze query performance metrics

6. REBUILD INDEXES (when needed):
   - After major data updates
   - When query patterns change
   - After schema modifications
   - When partition skew is detected
        """
        
        print(maintenance_guide)

class EcommerceIndexingStrategy:
    """
    Real-world example: Implementing indexing strategy for an e-commerce platform
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def create_ecommerce_data(self):
        """Create sample e-commerce data"""
        
        # Orders data
        orders_data = [
            (1001, 501, "2023-10-01", "Electronics", "Completed", 1299.99, "USA", "CA"),
            (1002, 502, "2023-10-01", "Clothing", "Pending", 89.99, "USA", "NY"),
            (1003, 503, "2023-10-02", "Electronics", "Shipped", 599.99, "UK", "London"),
            (1004, 501, "2023-10-02", "Books", "Completed", 29.99, "USA", "CA"),
            (1005, 504, "2023-10-03", "Electronics", "Completed", 899.99, "Canada", "ON"),
            (1006, 505, "2023-10-03", "Clothing", "Failed", 149.99, "USA", "TX"),
            (1007, 502, "2023-10-04", "Electronics", "Completed", 1599.99, "USA", "NY"),
            (1008, 506, "2023-10-04", "Books", "Shipped", 45.99, "UK", "Manchester"),
            (1009, 503, "2023-10-05", "Clothing", "Pending", 199.99, "UK", "London"),
            (1010, 507, "2023-10-05", "Electronics", "Completed", 799.99, "USA", "WA")
        ]
        
        orders_schema = StructType([
            StructField("order_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("customer_id", IntegerType(), False),
            StructField("order_date", StringType(), False),
            StructField("category", StringType(), False),
            StructField("status", StringType(), False),
            StructField("amount", DoubleType(), False),
            StructField("country", StringType(), False),
            StructField("region", StringType(), False)
        ])
        
        return self.spark.createDataFrame(orders_data, orders_schema)
    
    def implement_comprehensive_indexing(self, orders_df):
        """Implement comprehensive indexing strategy for e-commerce"""
        
        print("\nImplementing E-commerce Indexing Strategy...")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # 1. Single-column index for status queries (operational queries)
        print("\n1. Creating Single-Column Index for order status...")
        orders_df.write.mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("status") \
            .parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_status_index")
        print("   ✓ Status index created (for operational dashboards)")
        
        # 2. Multi-column index for analytics (country + category)
        print("\n2. Creating Multi-Column Index for geographic analytics...")
        orders_df.write.mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("country", "category") \
            .parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_geo_analytics_index")
        print("   ✓ Geographic analytics index created")
        
        # 3. Covering index for customer order history
        print("\n3. Creating Covering Index for customer queries...")
        customer_index = orders_df.select(
            "customer_id", "order_id", "order_date", 
            "category", "amount", "status"
        )
        customer_index.write.mode("overwrite") \
            .bucketBy(8, "customer_id") \
            .sortBy("order_date") \
            .saveAsTable("ecommerce_customer_orders")
        print("   ✓ Customer order history index created")
        
        # 4. Partial index for active orders only
        print("\n4. Creating Partial Index for active orders...")
        active_orders = orders_df.filter(col("status").isin(["Pending", "Shipped"]))
        active_orders.write.mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("status") \
            .parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_active_orders_index")
        print(f"   ✓ Active orders index created ({active_orders.count()} records)")
        
        # 5. Functional index with date parts and price tiers
        print("\n5. Creating Functional Index with computed columns...")
        functional_index = orders_df \
            .withColumn("order_year", year(col("order_date"))) \
            .withColumn("order_month", month(col("order_date"))) \
            .withColumn("price_tier",
                       when(col("amount") < 100, "Budget")
                       .when((col("amount") >= 100) & (col
```python
("amount") < 500), "Mid-Range")
                       .otherwise("Premium")) \
            .withColumn("order_day_of_week", dayofweek(col("order_date")))
        
        functional_index.write.mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("order_year", "order_month") \
            .parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_time_series_index")
        print("   ✓ Time-series functional index created")
        
        # 6. High-value orders index (partial + functional)
        print("\n6. Creating High-Value Orders Index...")
        high_value_index = functional_index.filter(col("amount") > 500) \
            .select("order_id", "customer_id", "order_date", "amount", 
                   "category", "status", "price_tier")
        
        high_value_index.write.mode("overwrite") \
            .partitionBy("category") \
            .sortBy(desc("amount")) \
            .parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_high_value_index")
        print(f"   ✓ High-value orders index created ({high_value_index.count()} records)")
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("E-commerce Indexing Strategy Implementation Complete!")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        return {
            'status_index': self.spark.read.parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_status_index"),
            'geo_analytics_index': self.spark.read.parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_geo_analytics_index"),
            'customer_index': self.spark.table("ecommerce_customer_orders"),
            'active_orders_index': self.spark.read.parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_active_orders_index"),
            'time_series_index': self.spark.read.parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_time_series_index"),
            'high_value_index': self.spark.read.parquet("/tmp/ecommerce_high_value_index")
        }
    
    def demonstrate_ecommerce_queries(self, indexes):
        """Demonstrate common e-commerce queries using different indexes"""
        
        print("\n" + "=" * 80)
        print("E-COMMERCE QUERY DEMONSTRATIONS")
        print("=" * 80)
        
        # Query 1: Operational dashboard - pending orders
        print("\n--- Query 1: Operational Dashboard (Pending Orders) ---")
        print("Using: Status Index (Single-Column)")
        
        pending_orders = indexes['status_index'].filter(col("status") == "Pending") \
            .select("order_id", "customer_id", "order_date", "amount", "country")
        
        pending_orders.show()
        print(f"Total pending orders: {pending_orders.count()}")
        
        # Query 2: Geographic sales analysis
        print("\n--- Query 2: Geographic Sales Analysis ---")
        print("Using: Geographic Analytics Index (Multi-Column)")
        
        geo_sales = indexes['geo_analytics_index'] \
            .groupBy("country", "category") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("order_count"),
                sum("amount").alias("total_revenue"),
                avg("amount").alias("avg_order_value")
            ) \
            .orderBy("country", "category")
        
        geo_sales.show()
        
        # Query 3: Customer order history
        print("\n--- Query 3: Customer Order History ---")
        print("Using: Customer Index (Covering Index with Bucketing)")
        
        customer_history = indexes['customer_index'] \
            .filter(col("customer_id") == 501) \
            .orderBy(desc("order_date"))
        
        customer_history.show()
        
        # Query 4: Active orders monitoring
        print("\n--- Query 4: Active Orders Monitoring ---")
        print("Using: Active Orders Index (Partial Index)")
        
        active_summary = indexes['active_orders_index'] \
            .groupBy("status") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("count"),
                sum("amount").alias("total_value")
            )
        
        active_summary.show()
        
        # Query 5: Monthly sales trends
        print("\n--- Query 5: Monthly Sales Trends ---")
        print("Using: Time-Series Index (Functional Index)")
        
        monthly_trends = indexes['time_series_index'] \
            .groupBy("order_year", "order_month") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("orders"),
                sum("amount").alias("revenue"),
                avg("amount").alias("avg_order")
            ) \
            .orderBy("order_year", "order_month")
        
        monthly_trends.show()
        
        # Query 6: Premium customer analysis
        print("\n--- Query 6: Premium Customer Analysis ---")
        print("Using: High-Value Orders Index (Partial + Functional)")
        
        premium_analysis = indexes['high_value_index'] \
            .groupBy("customer_id") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("high_value_orders"),
                sum("amount").alias("total_spent"),
                max("amount").alias("largest_order")
            ) \
            .orderBy(desc("total_spent"))
        
        premium_analysis.show()
        
        # Query 7: Day-of-week pattern analysis
        print("\n--- Query 7: Day-of-Week Pattern Analysis ---")
        print("Using: Time-Series Index (Functional Index)")
        
        dow_pattern = indexes['time_series_index'] \
            .groupBy("order_day_of_week") \
            .agg(
                count("*").alias("order_count"),
                avg("amount").alias("avg_amount")
            ) \
            .orderBy("order_day_of_week")
        
        dow_pattern.show()
        
        # Query 8: Price tier distribution
        print("\n--- Query 8: Price Tier Distribution ---")
        print("Using: Time-Series Index (Functional Index)")
        
        price_tier_dist = indexes['time_series_index'] \
            .groupBy("price_tier", "category") \
            .agg(count("*").alias("count")) \
            .orderBy("price_tier", "category")
        
        price_tier_dist.show()

summary = """

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
==============

1. SINGLE-COLUMN INDEX PATTERN
   ✓ Best for simple, single-condition filters
   ✓ Use partitioning for low-to-moderate cardinality columns
   ✓ Use bucketing for join optimization
   ✓ Example: Partition by status, department, or region

2. MULTI-COLUMN INDEX PATTERN
   ✓ Optimal for queries filtering on multiple columns
   ✓ Order columns by filter frequency (most frequent first)
   ✓ Avoid over-partitioning (keep partitions < 10,000)
   ✓ Example: Partition by (country, state) or (year, month)

3. COVERING INDEX PATTERN
   ✓ Eliminates joins by denormalizing data
   ✓ Cache frequently accessed views
   ✓ Pre-aggregate for analytics queries
   ✓ Example: Denormalized customer order view

4. PARTIAL INDEX PATTERN
   ✓ Index only relevant data subsets
   ✓ Reduces storage and maintenance costs
   ✓ Ideal for active/archived data separation
   ✓ Example: Index only pending/failed transactions

5. FUNCTIONAL INDEX PATTERN
   ✓ Pre-compute derived/transformed values
   ✓ Essential for case-insensitive searches
   ✓ Optimize date-based and mathematical queries
   ✓ Example: Add UPPER(name), YEAR(date), price_tier columns

6. SPATIAL INDEX PATTERN
   ✓ Critical for geographic/location queries
   ✓ Use geohashing for proximity searches
   ✓ Grid partitioning for bounding box queries
   ✓ Example: Store locator, delivery routing

PERFORMANCE RECOMMENDATIONS:
============================

FILE SIZE:
- Target 128MB - 1GB per file
- Use coalesce() to control file count
- Enable adaptive query execution

PARTITIONING:
- Keep partition count under 10,000
- Avoid small files (< 10MB)
- Partition on frequently filtered columns
- Use date-based partitioning for time-series

BUCKETING:
- Use power-of-2 bucket counts (4, 8, 16, 32)
- Bucket on join and aggregation keys
- Combine with sorting for compression

CACHING:
- Cache hot indexes in memory
- Use MEMORY_AND_DISK for large datasets
- Monitor cache usage and eviction
```

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession

# PATTERN 1: ALGEBRAIC REWRITE PATTERN
# ============================================================================
# Uses mathematical properties to transform queries into equivalent but more
# efficient forms (commutative, associative, distributive properties)

class AlgebraicRewritePattern:
    """
    Demonstrates algebraic query transformations using mathematical properties
    to optimize query execution plans.
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        
    def create_sample_data(self):
        """Create sample datasets for demonstration"""
        # Sales data
        sales_data = [
            (1, "Product_A", 100, 10, "2024-01-01"),
            (2, "Product_B", 200, 20, "2024-01-02"),
            (3, "Product_A", 150, 15, "2024-01-03"),
            (4, "Product_C", 300, 30, "2024-01-04"),
            (5, "Product_B", 250, 25, "2024-01-05")
        ]
        
        sales_schema = StructType([
            StructField("id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("product", StringType(), True),
            StructField("quantity", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("price", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("date", StringType(), True)
        ])
        
        return self.spark.createDataFrame(sales_data, sales_schema)
    
    def predicate_pushdown_example(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Algebraic Rewrite: Predicate Pushdown
        Transform: σ(p AND q)(R) → σ(p)(σ(q)(R))
        Push filters as close to data source as possible
        """
        print("\n=== ALGEBRAIC REWRITE: Predicate Pushdown ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Multiple filters applied together
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.filter((col("quantity") > 100) & (col("price") > 15))
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Filters pushed down and separated
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Predicate Pushdown):")
        result_after = df.filter(col("quantity") > 100).filter(col("price") > 15)
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def projection_pushdown_example(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Algebraic Rewrite: Projection Pushdown
        Transform: π(a,b)(σ(p)(R)) → π(a,b)(σ(p)(π(a,b,c)(R)))
        Select only required columns early
        """
        print("\n=== ALGEBRAIC REWRITE: Projection Pushdown ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Select all columns then filter
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.filter(col("quantity") > 100).select("product", "quantity")
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Project early to reduce data movement
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Projection Pushdown):")
        result_after = df.select("product", "quantity", "price") \
                         .filter(col("quantity") > 100) \
                         .select("product", "quantity")
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def commutative_join_reorder(self, df1: DataFrame, df2: DataFrame):
        """
        Algebraic Rewrite: Join Commutativity
        Transform: R ⋈ S = S ⋈ R
        Reorder joins based on cardinality
        """
        print("\n=== ALGEBRAIC REWRITE: Join Commutativity ===")
        
        # Create second dataset
        product_data = [
            ("Product_A", "Electronics"),
            ("Product_B", "Clothing"),
            ("Product_C", "Food")
        ]
        df2 = self.spark.createDataFrame(product_data, ["product", "category"])
        
        # BEFORE: Larger table first
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df1.join(df2, "product")
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Smaller table first (broadcast hint)
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Join Reordering):")
        result_after = df2.join(broadcast(df1), "product")
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def filter_distribution_example(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Algebraic Rewrite: Filter Distribution
        Transform: σ(p OR q)(R) → σ(p)(R) ∪ σ(q)(R)
        Distribute filters for parallel processing
        """
        print("\n=== ALGEBRAIC REWRITE: Filter Distribution ===")
        
        # BEFORE: OR condition
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.filter((col("product") == "Product_A") | (col("product") == "Product_B"))
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Distributed filters with union
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Filter Distribution):")
        result_a = df.filter(col("product") == "Product_A")
        result_b = df.filter(col("product") == "Product_B")
        result_after = result_a.union(result_b)
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after

class HeuristicRewritePattern:
    """

    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):

            (5, 105, 2500, "2024-01-05", "Electronics")
        ] * 100  # Multiply for larger dataset
        
        orders_schema = StructType([
            StructField("order_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("customer_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("amount", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("order_date", StringType(), True),
            StructField("category", StringType(), True)
        ])
        
        return self.spark.createDataFrame(orders_data, orders_schema)
    
    def early_filtering_heuristic(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Heuristic: Apply filters as early as possible
        Rule: Filters reduce data volume, apply before expensive operations
        """
        print("\n=== HEURISTIC REWRITE: Early Filtering ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Aggregate then filter
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        start_time = time.time()
        result_before = df.groupBy("category") \
                         .agg(sum("amount").alias("total_amount")) \
                         .filter(col("total_amount") > 100000)
        result_before.count()
        before_time = time.time() - start_time
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Filter then aggregate (when possible)
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Early Filtering):")
        start_time = time.time()
        result_after = df.filter(col("amount") > 1000) \
                        .groupBy("category") \
                        .agg(sum("amount").alias("total_amount"))
        result_after.count()
        after_time = time.time() - start_time
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        print(f"\nExecution time - Before: {before_time:.4f}s, After: {after_time:.4f}s")
        
        return result_after
    
    def avoid_cross_joins_heuristic(self, df1: DataFrame):
        """
        Heuristic: Avoid Cartesian products
        Rule: Cross joins are expensive, add join conditions
        """
        print("\n=== HEURISTIC REWRITE: Avoid Cross Joins ===")
        
        # Create second dataset
        categories_data = [("Electronics", 0.1), ("Clothing", 0.15), ("Food", 0.05)]
        df2 = self.spark.createDataFrame(categories_data, ["category", "discount"])
        
        # BEFORE: Cross join (bad practice)
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization (Cross Join - Avoid This!):")

        # result_before.explain(True)
        print("Cross join avoided in example due to performance concerns")
        
        # AFTER: Proper join with condition
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Proper Join):")
        result_after = df1.join(df2, "category", "inner")
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def partition_pruning_heuristic(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Heuristic: Use partition pruning
        Rule: Filter on partition columns first
        """
        print("\n=== HEURISTIC REWRITE: Partition Pruning ===")
        
        # Write data partitioned by category
        temp_path = "/tmp/partitioned_orders"
        df.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("category").parquet(temp_path)
        
        # Read partitioned data
        partitioned_df = self.spark.read.parquet(temp_path)
        
        # BEFORE: No partition filter
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = partitioned_df.filter(col("amount") > 2000)
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: With partition filter
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Partition Pruning):")
        result_after = partitioned_df.filter(
            (col("category") == "Electronics") & (col("amount") > 2000)
        )
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def broadcast_join_heuristic(self, df1: DataFrame):
        """
        Heuristic: Use broadcast joins for small tables
        Rule: If one table is small (<10MB), broadcast it
        """
        print("\n=== HEURISTIC REWRITE: Broadcast Join ===")
        
        # Small dimension table
        small_table_data = [
            ("Electronics", "High Value"),
            ("Clothing", "Medium Value"),
            ("Food", "Low Value")
        ]
        small_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(small_table_data, ["category", "value_tier"])
        
        # BEFORE: Regular join
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df1.join(small_df, "category")
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Broadcast join
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Broadcast Join):")
        result_after = df1.join(broadcast(small_df), "category")
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after

            ["category_id", "category_name", "department"]
        )

    def collect_statistics(self, df: DataFrame, name: str):

        row_count = df.count()

        stats = {
            "row_count": row_count,
            "size_bytes": size_in_bytes,
            "avg_row_size": size_in_bytes / row_count if row_count > 0 else 0
        }
        
        self.statistics_cache[name] = stats
        print(f"Statistics: {stats}")
        
        return stats
    
    def cost_based_join_order(self, large_df: DataFrame, medium_df: DataFrame, small_df: DataFrame):

        result_after = large_df \
            .join(broadcast(medium

            .join(broadcast(medium_df), large_df.product == medium_df.product_name) \
            .join(broadcast(small_df), medium_df.category == small_df.category_name)
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def selectivity_based_filter_order(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Cost-Based Rewrite: Filter Ordering by Selectivity
        Apply most selective filters first
        """
        print("\n=== COST-BASED REWRITE: Selectivity-Based Filter Ordering ===")
        
        # Calculate selectivity for different filters
        total_count = df.count()
        
        # Filter 1: amount > 50000 (low selectivity - few rows pass)
        filter1_count = df.filter(col("amount") > 50000).count()
        selectivity1 = filter1_count / total_count
        
        # Filter 2: date like '2024-01%' (high selectivity - many rows pass)
        filter2_count = df.filter(col("date").like("2024-01%")).count()
        selectivity2 = filter2_count / total_count
        
        print(f"\nFilter Selectivity Analysis:")
        print(f"Filter 1 (amount > 50000): {selectivity1:.4f} ({filter1_count} rows)")
        print(f"Filter 2 (date like '2024-01%'): {selectivity2:.4f} ({filter2_count} rows)")
        
        # BEFORE: High selectivity filter first (inefficient)
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.filter(col("date").like("2024-01%")) \
                         .filter(col("amount") > 50000)
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Low selectivity filter first (more efficient)
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Most Selective First):")
        result_after = df.filter(col("amount") > 50000) \
                        .filter(col("date").like("2024-01%"))
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def cost_based_aggregation_strategy(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Cost-Based Rewrite: Aggregation Strategy Selection
        Choose between hash vs sort-based aggregation
        """
        print("\n=== COST-BASED REWRITE: Aggregation Strategy ===")
        
        # Estimate cardinality of group by key
        distinct_products = df.select("product").distinct().count()
        total_rows = df.count()
        cardinality_ratio = distinct_products / total_rows
        
        print(f"\nCardinality Analysis:")
        print(f"Distinct products: {distinct_products}")
        print(f"Total rows: {total_rows}")
        print(f"Cardinality ratio: {cardinality_ratio:.4f}")
        
        # BEFORE: Default aggregation
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.groupBy("product").agg(
            sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
            count("*").alias("order_count")
        )
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Optimized with repartition hint based on cardinality
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Cardinality-Based Strategy):")
        if cardinality_ratio < 0.1:  # Low cardinality
            # Use fewer partitions for low cardinality
            result_after = df.repartition(10, "product").groupBy("product").agg(
                sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
                count("*").alias("order_count")
            )
        else:  # High cardinality
            # Use more partitions for high cardinality
            result_after = df.repartition(100, "product").groupBy("product").agg(
                sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
                count("*").alias("order_count")
            )
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after

# Uses predefined transformation rules to optimize queries

class RuleBasedRewritePattern:
    """
    Implements rule-based query optimization using transformation rules
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        self.rules = []
        self._initialize_rules()
        
    def _initialize_rules(self):
        """Initialize optimization rules"""
        self.rules = [
            {"name": "Constant Folding", "priority": 1},
            {"name": "Predicate Pushdown", "priority": 2},
            {"name": "Column Pruning", "priority": 3},
            {"name": "Null Propagation", "priority": 4},
            {"name": "Boolean Simplification", "priority": 5}
        ]
    
    def create_sample_data(self):
        """Create sample datasets"""
        data = [
            (1, "Alice", 25, 50000, "Engineering", True),
            (2, "Bob", 30, 60000, "Sales", True),
            (3, "Charlie", 35, 70000, "Engineering", False),
            (4, "David", 28, 55000, "Marketing", True),
            (5, "Eve", 32, 65000, "Sales", None)
        ]
        
        schema = StructType([
            StructField("id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("age", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("salary", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("department", StringType(), True),
            StructField("is_active", BooleanType(), True)
        ])
        
        return self.spark.createDataFrame(data, schema)
    
    def constant_folding_rule(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Rule: Constant Folding
        Transform: WHERE col > 5 + 5 → WHERE col > 10
        Evaluate constant expressions at compile time
        """
        print("\n=== RULE-BASED REWRITE: Constant Folding ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Expression with constants
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.filter(col("salary") > lit(50000) + lit(10000))
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Folded constant
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Constant Folding):")
        result_after = df.filter(col("salary") > 60000)
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def null_propagation_rule(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Rule: Null Propagation
        Transform: NULL + x → NULL, NULL AND x → NULL
        Simplify expressions involving NULL
        """
        print("\n=== RULE-BASED REWRITE: Null Propagation ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Complex null handling
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.withColumn(
            "computed",
            when(col("is_active").isNull(), None)
            .otherwise(col("is_active") & lit(True))
        )
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Simplified null handling
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Null Propagation):")
        result_after = df.withColumn(
            "computed",
            col("is_active")  # Simplified since AND True doesn't change value
        )
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def boolean_simplification_rule(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Rule: Boolean Simplification
        Transform: WHERE (a AND TRUE) OR (b AND FALSE) → WHERE a
        Simplify boolean expressions
        """
        print("\n=== RULE-BASED REWRITE: Boolean Simplification ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Complex boolean expression
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.filter(
            ((col("age") > 25) & lit(True)) | ((col("age") < 20) & lit(False))
        )
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Simplified boolean expression
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Boolean Simplification):")
        result_after = df.filter(col("age") > 25)
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def redundant_operation_elimination_rule(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Rule: Redundant Operation Elimination
        Transform: SELECT DISTINCT * FROM (SELECT DISTINCT * FROM T) → SELECT DISTINCT * FROM T
        Remove redundant operations
        """
        print("\n=== RULE-BASED REWRITE: Redundant Operation Elimination ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Redundant distinct operations
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = df.select("department").distinct().distinct()
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Single distinct operation
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Redundancy Removed):")
        result_after = df.select("department").distinct()
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def subquery_unnesting_rule(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Rule: Subquery Unnesting
        Transform: Correlated subqueries to joins
        """
        print("\n=== RULE-BASED REWRITE: Subquery Unnesting ===")
        
        # Create department summary
        dept_summary = df.groupBy("department").agg(
            avg("salary").alias("avg_salary")
        )
        
        # BEFORE: Conceptual correlated subquery (simulated)
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization (Conceptual Correlated Subquery):")
        print("SELECT * FROM employees e WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department = e.department)")
        
        # AFTER: Unnested to join
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Unnested to Join):")
        result_after = df.join(
            dept_summary,
            "department"
        ).filter(col("salary") > col("avg_salary"))
        result_after.explain(True)
        result_after.show()
        
        return result_after


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 5: SEMANTIC REWRITE PATTERN
# ============================================================================
# Uses semantic knowledge about data and business logic to optimize queries

class SemanticRewritePattern:
    """
    Implements semantic-based query optimization using domain knowledge
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        self.semantic_rules = {}
        self._initialize_semantic_knowledge()
        
    def _initialize_semantic_knowledge(self):
        """Initialize semantic knowledge base"""
        self.semantic_rules = {
            "functional_dependencies": {
                "employee_id": ["name", "department", "manager_id"],
                "department": ["department_head", "location"]
            },
            "constraints": {
                "age": {"min": 18, "max": 65},
                "salary": {"min": 30000, "max": 200000}
            },
            "relationships": {
                "employee_department": "many_to_one",
                "department_location": "one_to_one"
            }
        }
    
    def create_sample_data(self):
        """Create sample datasets with semantic relationships"""
        # Employee data
        employee_data = [
            (1, "Alice", 28, 75000, "Engineering", 10, 1001),
            (2, "Bob", 32, 85000, "Engineering", 10, 1001),
            (3, "Charlie", 45, 95000, "Sales", 20, 1002),
            (4, "David", 29, 70000, "Sales", 20, 1002),
            (5, "Eve", 35, 90000, "Marketing", 30, 1003)
        ]
        
        employee_schema = StructType([
            StructField("emp_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("age", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("salary", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("department", StringType(), True),
            StructField("dept_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("manager_id", IntegerType(), True)
        ])
        
        employees = self.spark.createDataFrame(employee_data, employee_schema)
        
        # Department data
        dept_data = [
            (10, "Engineering", "Building A", 1001),
            (20, "Sales", "Building B", 1002),
            (30, "Marketing", "Building C", 1003)
        ]
        
        dept_schema = StructType([
            StructField("dept_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("dept_name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("location", StringType(), True),
            StructField("head_id", IntegerType(), True)
        ])
        
        departments = self.spark.createDataFrame(dept_data, dept_schema)
        
        return employees, departments
    
    def functional_dependency_rewrite(self, employees: DataFrame, departments: DataFrame):
        """
        Semantic Rewrite: Functional Dependency Elimination
        Remove redundant joins using functional dependencies
        """
        print("\n=== SEMANTIC REWRITE: Functional Dependency Optimization ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Join with department table to get dept_name (redundant)
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        print("Joining with departments to get dept_name when it's already in employees")
        result_before = employees.join(
            departments,
            employees.dept_id == departments.dept_id
        ).select(
            employees.emp_id,
            employees.name,
            departments.dept_name
        )
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Use existing department column (functional dependency)
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Using Functional Dependency):")
        print("Using department column directly from employees table")
        result_after = employees.select(
            col("emp_id"),
            col("name"),
            col("department").alias("dept_name")
        )
        result_after.explain(True)
        result_after.show()
        
        return result_after
    
    def constraint_based_rewrite(self, employees: DataFrame):
        """
        Semantic Rewrite: Constraint-Based Simplification
        Use constraints to simplify or eliminate conditions
        """
        print("\n=== SEMANTIC REWRITE: Constraint-Based Simplification ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Redundant filter based on constraints
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        print("Filtering age > 10 when constraint ensures age >= 18")
        result_before = employees.filter(
            (col("age") > 10) & (col("age") < 70)
        )
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Simplified using semantic constraints
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Using Constraints):")
        print("Simplified to age < 70 since age > 10 is always true given constraint age >= 18")
        result_after = employees.filter(col("age") < 70)
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def relationship_aware_rewrite(self, employees: DataFrame, departments: DataFrame):
        """
```python
        Semantic Rewrite: Relationship-Aware Optimization
        Use cardinality relationships to optimize joins
        """
        print("\n=== SEMANTIC REWRITE: Relationship-Aware Optimization ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Regular join without leveraging relationship knowledge
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        print("Regular join without considering many-to-one relationship")
        result_before = employees.join(
            departments,
            employees.dept_id == departments.dept_id,
            "inner"
        )
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Optimized using relationship knowledge (many-to-one)
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Relationship-Aware):")
        print("Broadcast join since departments is dimension table (one side of many-to-one)")
        result_after = employees.join(
            broadcast(departments),
            employees.dept_id == departments.dept_id,
            "inner"
        )
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        return result_after
    
    def semantic_aggregation_rewrite(self, employees: DataFrame):
        """
        Semantic Rewrite: Aggregation Optimization Using Domain Knowledge
        Simplify aggregations using business logic
        """
        print("\n=== SEMANTIC REWRITE: Semantic Aggregation Optimization ===")
        
        # BEFORE: Count distinct departments by joining
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        result_before = employees.groupBy("dept_id").agg(
            countDistinct("department").alias("dept_count")
        )
        result_before.explain(True)
        result_before.show()
        
        # AFTER: Simplified using functional dependency knowledge
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Using Semantic Knowledge):")
        print("Since dept_id -> department (functional dependency), count is always 1")
        result_after = employees.groupBy("dept_id").agg(
            lit(1).alias("dept_count"),
            first("department").alias("department_name")
        )
        result_after.explain(True)
        result_after.show()
        
        return result_after
    
    def temporal_semantic_rewrite(self):
        """
        Semantic Rewrite: Temporal Logic Optimization
        Use temporal semantics to optimize time-based queries
        """
        print("\n=== SEMANTIC REWRITE: Temporal Semantic Optimization ===")
        
        # Create temporal data
        temporal_data = [
            (1, "2024-01-01", "2024-01-31", "Active"),
            (2, "2024-02-01", "2024-02-28", "Active"),
            (3, "2024-03-01", "2024-03-31", "Inactive"),
            (4, "2024-01-15", "2024-02-15", "Active")
        ]
        
        temporal_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(
            temporal_data,
            ["id", "start_date", "end_date", "status"]
        )
        
        # BEFORE: Complex date range check
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        query_date = "2024-01-20"
        result_before = temporal_df.filter(
            (col("start_date") <= query_date) & 
            (col("end_date") >= query_date) &
            (col("status") == "Active")
        )
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Optimized using temporal semantics
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Temporal Semantics):")
        print("Pre-filter on status first (more selective), then date range")
        result_after = temporal_df.filter(col("status") == "Active") \
                                  .filter(
                                      (col("start_date") <= query_date) & 
                                      (col("end_date") >= query_date)
                                  )
        result_after.explain(True)
        result_after.show()
        
        return result_after
    
    def view_materialization_rewrite(self, employees: DataFrame):
        """
        Semantic Rewrite: Materialized View Substitution
        Replace complex queries with pre-computed results
        """
        print("\n=== SEMANTIC REWRITE: Materialized View Substitution ===")
        
        # Create materialized view (pre-aggregated data)
        print("\nCreating Materialized View...")
        materialized_view = employees.groupBy("department").agg(
            avg("salary").alias("avg_salary"),
            count("*").alias("emp_count"),
            max("salary").alias("max_salary"),
            min("salary").alias("min_salary")
        ).cache()  # Cache to simulate materialization
        
        materialized_view.count()  # Force materialization
        
        # BEFORE: Compute aggregation on-the-fly
        print("\nBEFORE Optimization:")
        start_time = time.time()
        result_before = employees.groupBy("department").agg(
            avg("salary").alias("avg_salary")
        ).filter(col("avg_salary") > 70000)
        result_before.show()
        before_time = time.time() - start_time
        result_before.explain(True)
        
        # AFTER: Use materialized view
        print("\nAFTER Optimization (Using Materialized View):")
        start_time = time.time()
        result_after = materialized_view.filter(col("avg_salary") > 70000)
        result_after.show()
        after_time = time.time() - start_time
        result_after.explain(True)
        
        print(f"\nExecution time - Before: {before_time:.4f}s, After: {after_time:.4f}s")
        
        materialized_view.unpersist()
        
        return result_after


# ============================================================================
# MAIN EXECUTION AND DEMONSTRATION
# ============================================================================

def main():
    """
    Main function to demonstrate all query rewrite patterns
    """
    
    # Initialize Spark Session with optimizations enabled
    spark = SparkSession.builder \
        .appName("Query Rewrite Strategy Patterns") \
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") \
        .config("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", "true") \
        .config("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "10485760") \
        .config("spark.sql.cbo.enabled", "true") \
        .config("spark.sql.statistics.histogram.enabled", "true") \
        .master("local[*]") \
        .getOrCreate()
    
    spark.sparkContext.setLogLevel("ERROR")
    
    print("="*80)
    print("QUERY REWRITE STRATEGY PATTERNS DEMONSTRATION")
    print("="*80)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # PATTERN 1: ALGEBRAIC REWRITE PATTERN
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 1: ALGEBRAIC REWRITE PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    print("Uses mathematical properties (commutative, associative, distributive)")
    print("to transform queries into equivalent but more efficient forms")
    
    algebraic = AlgebraicRewritePattern(spark)
    sales_df = algebraic.create_sample_data()
    
    algebraic.predicate_pushdown_example(sales_df)
    algebraic.projection_pushdown_example(sales_df)
    algebraic.commutative_join_reorder(sales_df, None)
    algebraic.filter_distribution_example(sales_df)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # PATTERN 2: HEURISTIC REWRITE PATTERN
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 2: HEURISTIC REWRITE PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    print("Uses rule-of-thumb strategies based on common optimization practices")
    
    heuristic = HeuristicRewritePattern(spark)
    orders_df = heuristic.create_sample_data()
    
    heuristic.early_filtering_heuristic(orders_df)
    heuristic.avoid_cross_joins_heuristic(orders_df)
    heuristic.partition_pruning_heuristic(orders_df)
    heuristic.broadcast_join_heuristic(orders_df)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # PATTERN 3: COST-BASED REWRITE PATTERN
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 3: COST-BASED REWRITE PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    print("Uses statistics and cost estimation to choose optimal query plans")
    
    cost_based = CostBasedRewritePattern(spark)
    large_df, medium_df, small_df = cost_based.create_sample_data()
    
    cost_based.cost_based_join_order(large_df, medium_df, small_df)
    cost_based.selectivity_based_filter_order(large_df)
    cost_based.cost_based_aggregation_strategy(large_df)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # PATTERN 4: RULE-BASED REWRITE PATTERN
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 4: RULE-BASED REWRITE PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    print("Uses predefined transformation rules to optimize queries")
    
    rule_based = RuleBasedRewritePattern(spark)
    emp_df = rule_based.create_sample_data()
    
    rule_based.constant_folding_rule(emp_df)
    rule_based.null_propagation_rule(emp_df)
    rule_based.boolean_simplification_rule(emp_df)
    rule_based.redundant_operation_elimination_rule(emp_df)
    rule_based.subquery_unnesting_rule(emp_df)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # PATTERN 5: SEMANTIC REWRITE PATTERN
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("PATTERN 5: SEMANTIC REWRITE PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    print("Uses semantic knowledge about data and business logic to optimize")
    
    semantic = SemanticRewritePattern(spark)
    employees_df, departments_df = semantic.create_sample_data()
    
    semantic.functional_dependency_rewrite(employees_df, departments_df)
    semantic.constraint_based_rewrite(employees_df)
    semantic.relationship_aware_rewrite(employees_df, departments_df)
    semantic.semantic_aggregation_rewrite(employees_df)
    semantic.temporal_semantic_rewrite()
    semantic.view_materialization_rewrite(employees_df)
    
    # ========================================================================
    # SUMMARY AND BEST PRACTICES
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("SUMMARY: WHEN TO USE EACH PATTERN")
    print("="*80)
    
    summary = """
    1. ALGEBRAIC REWRITE PATTERN
       - Use when: Working with relational algebra operations
       - Best for: Filter pushdown, projection pruning, join reordering
       - Benefits: Mathematically proven equivalence, always safe
    
    2. HEURISTIC REWRITE PATTERN
       - Use when: Quick optimizations needed without detailed statistics
       - Best for: Early filtering, avoiding cross joins, partition pruning
       - Benefits: Fast to apply, low overhead, generally effective
    
    3. COST-BASED REWRITE PATTERN
       - Use when: Statistics are available and query complexity is high
       - Best for: Join order selection, aggregation strategy, multi-way joins
       - Benefits: Optimal plans for complex queries, adapts to data distribution
    
    4. RULE-BASED REWRITE PATTERN
       - Use when: Applying standard transformations and simplifications
       - Best for: Constant folding, boolean simplification, redundancy elimination
       - Benefits: Predictable, easy to understand, no statistics needed
    
    5. SEMANTIC REWRITE PATTERN
       - Use when: Domain knowledge and constraints are available
       - Best for: Functional dependencies, constraint-based optimization
       - Benefits: Leverages business logic, can eliminate unnecessary operations
    
    BEST PRACTICES:
    - Combine multiple patterns for maximum optimization
    - Apply patterns in order: Semantic → Algebraic → Heuristic → Cost-Based → Rule-Based
    - Always verify query correctness after rewrites
    - Monitor performance metrics to validate optimizations
    - Keep statistics up-to-date for cost-based optimizations
    - Document semantic rules and constraints for maintainability
    """
    
    print(summary)
    
    # Cleanup
    spark.stop()
    
    print("\n" + "="*80)
    print("DEMONSTRATION COMPLETE")
    print("="*80)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

class QueryRewriteAnalyzer:
    """

    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):

    def analyze_plan_complexity(self, df: DataFrame) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """

        """
        plan = df._jdf.queryExecution().analyzed().toString()
        
        metrics = {
            "num_joins": plan.count("Join"),
            "num_filters": plan.count("Filter"),
            "num_aggregates": plan.count("Aggregate"),
            "num_projects": plan.count("Project"),
            "num_exchanges": plan.count("Exchange"),
            "plan_depth": plan.count("\n"),
            "has_broadcast": "BroadcastExchange" in plan,
            "has_sort": "Sort" in plan
        }
        
        return metrics

        """

        for key in metrics_before.keys():

        )

class PatternRecommendationEngine:
    """
    Recommends appropriate rewrite patterns based on query characteristics
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        self.recommendations = []
        
    def analyze_query_characteristics(self, df: DataFrame) -> Dict[str, Any]:
        """
        Analyze query to determine its characteristics
        """
        plan_str = df._jdf.queryExecution().analyzed().toString()
        
        characteristics = {
            "has_joins": "Join" in plan_str,
            "has_aggregations": "Aggregate" in plan_str,
            "has_filters": "Filter" in plan_str,
            "has_subqueries": "Subquery" in plan_str,
            "has_unions": "Union" in plan_str,
            "has_window_functions": "Window" in plan_str,
            "complexity_score": plan_str.count("\n")
        }
        
        return characteristics
    
    def recommend_patterns(self, df: DataFrame) -> List[Dict[str, str]]:
        """
        Recommend rewrite patterns based on query analysis
        """
        characteristics = self.analyze_query_characteristics(df)
        recommendations = []
        
        # Algebraic patterns
        if characteristics["has_filters"] and characteristics["has_joins"]:
            recommendations.append({
                "pattern": "Algebraic Rewrite",
                "technique": "Predicate Pushdown",
                "reason": "Query has filters and joins - push filters closer to data source",
                "priority": "High"
            })
        
        # Heuristic patterns
        if characteristics["has_joins"]:
            recommendations.append({
                "pattern": "Heuristic Rewrite",
                "technique": "Broadcast Join",
                "reason": "Query has joins - consider broadcasting small tables",
                "priority": "Medium"
            })
        
        # Cost-based patterns
        if characteristics["complexity_score"] > 10:
            recommendations.append({
                "pattern": "Cost-Based Rewrite",
                "technique": "Join Order Optimization",
                "reason": "Complex query detected - use statistics for optimal join order",
                "priority": "High"
            })
        
        # Rule-based patterns
        if characteristics["has_subqueries"]:
            recommendations.append({
                "pattern": "Rule-Based Rewrite",
                "technique": "Subquery Unnesting",
                "reason": "Query has subqueries - consider unnesting to joins",
                "priority": "Medium"
            })
        
        # Semantic patterns
        if characteristics["has_aggregations"]:
            recommendations.append({
                "pattern": "Semantic Rewrite",
                "technique": "Materialized View Substitution",
                "reason": "Query has aggregations - consider pre-computed views",
                "priority": "Low"
            })
        
        return recommendations
    
    def print_recommendations(self, df: DataFrame):
        """
        Print formatted recommendations for a query
        """
        recommendations = self.recommend_patterns(df)
        
        print("\n=== PATTERN RECOMMENDATIONS ===")
        print(f"Total Recommendations: {len(recommendations)}\n")
        
        for i, rec in enumerate(recommendations, 1):
            print(f"{i}. {rec['pattern']} - {rec['technique']}")
            print(f"   Priority: {rec['priority']}")
            print(f"   Reason: {rec['reason']}\n")

# BONUS: COMPREHENSIVE EXAMPLE WITH ALL PATTERNS

class ComprehensiveRewriteExample:
    """
    Demonstrates combining multiple rewrite patterns for maximum optimization
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark: SparkSession):
        self.spark = spark
        
    def create_comprehensive_dataset(self):
        """
        Create a realistic dataset for comprehensive optimization
        """
        # Large sales fact table
        sales_data = [
            (i, 
             f"Product_{i % 1000}", 
             i % 100, 
             i % 50, 
             (i % 10) * 100, 
             f"2024-{(i % 12) + 1:02d}-{(i % 28) + 1:02d}",
             f"Region_{i % 5}",
             i % 3 == 0) 
            for i in range(10000)
        ]
        
        sales_schema = StructType([
            StructField("sale_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("product_name", StringType(), True),
            StructField("customer_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("store_id", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("amount", IntegerType(), True),
            StructField("sale_date", StringType(), True),
            StructField("region", StringType(), True),
            StructField("is_online", BooleanType(), True)
        ])
        
        sales_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(sales_data, sales_schema)
        
        # Product dimension table
        product_data = [
            (f"Product_{i}", f"Category_{i % 20}", i * 10, f"Brand_{i % 10}")
            for i in range(1000)
        ]
        products_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(
            product_data,
            ["product_name", "category", "base_price", "brand"]
        )
        
        # Store dimension table
        store_data = [
            (i, f"Store_{i}", f"Region_{i % 5}", f"City_{i % 20}")
            for i in range(50)
        ]
        stores_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(
            store_data,
            ["store_id", "store_name", "region", "city"]
        )
        
        return sales_df, products_df, stores_df
    
    def unoptimized_query(self, sales_df: DataFrame, products_df: DataFrame, stores_df: DataFrame):
        """
        Complex query WITHOUT optimizations
        """

    def optimized_query(self, sales_df: DataFrame, products_df: DataFrame, stores_df: DataFrame):
        """
