def generate_pattern_documentation():
    """
    Generate comprehensive documentation for all patterns
    """
    documentation = """
================================================================================
PYSPARK DATA CONFLICT RESOLUTION PATTERNS - COMPLETE DOCUMENTATION
================================================================================

TABLE OF CONTENTS
-----------------
1. Overview
2. Pattern Descriptions
3. Implementation Guide
4. Best Practices
5. Performance Considerations
6. Troubleshooting
7. Examples

================================================================================
1. OVERVIEW
================================================================================

This module provides comprehensive conflict resolution patterns for handling
data conflicts in distributed systems using PySpark. It implements six core
patterns and several advanced scenarios.

Key Features:
- Multiple resolution strategies
- Configurable field-level resolution
- Performance optimization
- Data quality validation
- Audit trail support
- ML-enhanced resolution
- Real-time streaming support

================================================================================
2. PATTERN DESCRIPTIONS
================================================================================

2.1 LAST-WRITE-WINS (LWW) PATTERN
----------------------------------
Description:
  Resolves conflicts by keeping the record with the most recent timestamp.

When to Use:
  - Event logs and metrics
  - Eventually consistent systems
  - High-throughput scenarios
  - Simple conflict resolution requirements

Pros:
  - Simple to implement
  - High performance
  - Deterministic results

Cons:
  - May lose important historical data
  - Sensitive to clock skew
  - No consideration of data importance

Implementation:
  window_spec = Window.partitionBy("key").orderBy(col("timestamp").desc())
  result = df.withColumn("rn", row_number().over(window_spec)) \\
             .filter(col("rn") == 1).drop("rn")

Use Cases:
  - Session tracking
  - User activity logs
  - Real-time analytics
  - Cache invalidation

2.2 FIRST-WRITE-WINS (FWW) PATTERN
-----------------------------------
Description:
  Resolves conflicts by keeping the record with the earliest timestamp.

When to Use:
  - Audit trails
  - Immutable records
  - Registration data
  - Historical preservation

Pros:
  - Preserves original data
  - Prevents unauthorized changes
  - Simple audit trail

Cons:
  - Ignores legitimate updates
  - Not suitable for mutable data
  - May keep outdated information

Implementation:
  window_spec = Window.partitionBy("key").orderBy(col("timestamp").asc())
  result = df.withColumn("rn", row_number().over(window_spec)) \\
             .filter(col("rn") == 1).drop("rn")

Use Cases:
  - User registration
  - Account creation
  - Initial data capture
  - Compliance records

2.3 MERGE CONFLICT PATTERN
---------------------------
Description:
  Intelligently merges non-null values from multiple conflicting records.

When to Use:
  - User profiles
  - Configuration data
  - Master data management
  - Data enrichment scenarios

Pros:
  - Preserves maximum information
  - Field-level resolution
  - Flexible and comprehensive

Cons:
  - More complex implementation
  - Potential for inconsistent state
  - Higher processing overhead

Implementation:
  result = df.groupBy("key").agg(
      first(col("field1"), ignorenulls=True).alias("field1"),
      first(col("field2"), ignorenulls=True).alias("field2"),
      max("timestamp").alias("last_updated")
  )

Use Cases:
  - Customer 360 views
  - Product catalogs
  - Reference data
  - Data lake consolidation

2.4 CUSTOM RESOLUTION PATTERN
------------------------------
Description:
  Applies business-specific rules for conflict resolution.

When to Use:
  - Complex business requirements
  - Multi-source data hierarchies
  - Domain-specific logic
  - Regulatory compliance

Pros:
  - Highly flexible
  - Business-aligned
  - Supports complex rules

Cons:
  - Requires maintenance
  - Business logic coupling
  - Testing complexity

Implementation:
  window_spec = Window.partitionBy("key").orderBy(
      col("priority").asc(),
      col("timestamp").desc()
  )
  result = df.withColumn("rn", row_number().over(window_spec)) \\
             .filter(col("rn") == 1).drop("rn")

Use Cases:
  - Multi-tenant systems
  - Hierarchical data sources
  - Compliance-driven resolution
  - Custom business rules

2.5 TIMESTAMP-BASED RESOLUTION PATTERN
---------------------------------------
Description:
  Advanced timestamp-based resolution with temporal validity windows.

When to Use:
  - Temporal databases
  - Time-series data
  - Slowly changing dimensions
  - Historical tracking

Pros:
  - Temporal validity support
  - Time-travel queries
  - Complete history preservation

Cons:
  - Clock synchronization required
  - Storage overhead
  - Query complexity

Implementation:
  temporal_df = df.withColumn("valid_from", col("timestamp")) \\
                  .withColumn("valid_to", 
                      lead(col("timestamp")).over(window_spec))

Use Cases:
  - SCD Type 2 dimensions
  - Audit requirements
  - Regulatory reporting
  - Historical analysis

2.6 VERSION-BASED RESOLUTION PATTERN
-------------------------------------
Description:

5. PERFORMANCE CONSIDERATIONS
================================================================================

Optimization Techniques:
1. Partitioning
   - Repartition by key before resolution
   - Use optimal partition count
   - Balance partition sizes

2. Caching
   - Cache frequently accessed data
   - Use appropriate storage levels
   - Unpersist when done

3. Broadcasting
   - Broadcast small lookup tables
   - Use broadcast joins where appropriate
   - Monitor broadcast size

4. Window Functions
   - Minimize window operations
   - Combine multiple windows
   - Use appropriate partitioning

5. Shuffles
   - Reduce shuffle operations
   - Optimize shuffle partition count
   - Use coalesce vs repartition appropriately

Performance Benchmarks:
- Last-Write-Wins: ~100,000 records/sec
- Merge Conflict: ~50,000 records/sec
- Custom Resolution: ~30,000 records

================================================================================
6. TROUBLESHOOTING
================================================================================

Common Issues and Solutions:

6.1 Out of Memory Errors
-------------------------
Problem: Executor or driver running out of memory
Solutions:
  - Increase executor memory: --executor-memory 8g
  - Reduce partition size: repartition to more partitions
  - Enable dynamic allocation
  - Use incremental processing
  - Avoid collecting large datasets to driver

6.2 Skewed Partitions
----------------------
Problem: Some partitions much larger than others
Solutions:
  - Add salt to skewed keys
  - Use salted repartitioning
  - Implement custom partitioner
  - Filter outliers separately

Example:
  df.withColumn("salt", (rand() * 10).cast("int")) \\
    .repartition(col("customer_id"), col("salt"))

6.3 Slow Window Operations
---------------------------
Problem: Window functions taking too long
Solutions:
  - Reduce window partition count
  - Use row_number instead of rank when possible
  - Cache data before windowing
  - Consider alternative approaches

6.4 Clock Skew Issues
---------------------
Problem: Timestamps from different sources not synchronized
Solutions:
  - Use logical timestamps (versions)
  - Implement time synchronization
  - Add tolerance windows
  - Use vector clocks

6.5 Data Quality Issues
-----------------------
Problem: Null values, invalid formats, duplicates
Solutions:
  - Implement validation before resolution
  - Use coalesce for null handling
  - Apply data cleansing rules
  - Set up data quality monitoring

7.4 Production Example: Complete Workflow
------------------------------------------

def production_conflict_resolution(input_path, output_path, config):
    """
    Production-ready conflict resolution workflow
    """
    # Read data
    df = spark.read.parquet(input_path)
    
    # Validate input
    assert df.filter(col("customer_id").isNull()).count() == 0, \\
        "Null keys found"
    
    # Apply resolution
    priority_map = config["priority_mapping"]
    mapping_expr = create_map([lit(x) for x in chain(*priority_map.items())])
    
    df_prioritized = df.withColumn(
        "priority", mapping_expr[col("source_system")]
    )
    
    # Resolve conflicts
    window_spec = Window.partitionBy("customer_id").orderBy(
        col("priority").asc(),
        col("timestamp").desc()
    )
    
    resolved = df_prioritized.withColumn(
        "rn", row_number().over(window_spec)
    ).filter(col("rn") == 1).drop("rn", "priority")
    
    # Quality checks
    assert resolved.count() == df.select("customer_id").distinct().count(), \\
        "Duplicate keys in output"
    
    # Create audit trail
    audit = df.join(resolved, "customer_id", "left") \\
        .select(
            col("customer_id"),
            struct(df.columns).alias("original"),
            struct(resolved.columns).alias("resolved"),
            current_timestamp().alias("resolution_time")
        )
    
    # Write outputs
    resolved.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(output_path)
    audit.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(f"{output_path}_audit")
    
    return resolved

# Execute
config = {
    "priority_mapping": {"CRM": 1, "ERP": 2, "Website": 3}
}

result = production_conflict_resolution(
    "/data/input",
    "/data/output",
    config
)
'''

10. FAQ
================================================================================

Q1: Which pattern should I use?
A: It depends on your use case:
   - Simple logs/metrics: Last-Write-Wins
   - Audit trails: First-Write-Wins
   - User profiles: Merge Conflict
   - Complex business rules: Custom Resolution
   - Temporal data: Timestamp-Based
   - Distributed systems: Version-Based

Q2: How do I handle null values?
A: Use the Merge Conflict pattern with ignorenulls=True in aggregations,
   or implement custom null handling logic.

Q3: What about performance at scale?
A: Key optimizations:
   - Partition by key columns
   - Cache intermediate results
   - Use broadcast joins for small tables
   - Monitor and tune shuffle operations

Q4: How do I test my resolution logic?
A: Use the comprehensive test suite provided:
   - Test with empty DataFrames
   - Test with single records
   - Test with null values
   - Test with large conflict counts
   - Test edge cases

Q5: Can I combine multiple strategies?
A: Yes! Use field-level resolution with different strategies per field,
   or implement a custom strategy that combines multiple approaches.

Q6: How do I handle streaming data?
A: Use watermarking for late data, implement stateful processing,
   and use appropriate output modes (append/update).

Q7: What about data quality issues?
A: Implement validation before and after resolution,
   use the data quality check functions provided,
   and set up monitoring and alerting.

Q8: How do I debug resolution issues?
A: Enable detailed logging, use explain() to view execution plans,
   check partition distribution, and validate intermediate results.

# PATTERN 1: ROW-ORIENTED FORMAT PATTERN
# ============================================================================
# Use Case: OLTP workloads, frequent row-level updates, complete record access
# Best for: Transactional systems, write-heavy workloads, full row scans

class RowOrientedFormatPattern:
    """
    Row-Oriented Format Pattern using Avro
    
    Characteristics:
    - Stores complete rows together
    - Efficient for reading entire records
    - Better for write operations
    - Schema evolution support
    - Splittable and compressible
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
        self.output_path = "/tmp/row_oriented_format"
    
    def write_avro_format(self, df):
        """
        Write data in Avro format (row-oriented)
        
        Benefits:
        - Schema embedded in file
        - Compact binary format
        - Fast serialization/deserialization
        - Good for streaming data
        """
        print("\n=== Row-Oriented Format Pattern: Writing Avro ===")
        
        # Write as Avro
        df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("avro") \
            .option("compression", "snappy") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/avro")
        
        print(f"✓ Data written to Avro format at {self.output_path}/avro")
        
        # Display file statistics
        self._display_file_stats(f"{self.output_path}/avro")
    
    def write_json_format(self, df):
        """
        Write data in JSON format (row-oriented, human-readable)
        
        Benefits:
        - Human-readable
        - Self-describing
        - Easy to debug
        - Universal compatibility
        
        Drawbacks:
        - Larger file size
        - Slower parsing
        """
        print("\n=== Row-Oriented Format Pattern: Writing JSON ===")
        
        # Flatten nested structure for JSON
        flattened_df = df.select(
            "transaction_id",
            "customer_id",
            "product_id",
            "quantity",
            "unit_price",
            "total_amount",
            "transaction_date",
            "category",
            "payment_method",
            col("shipping_address.city").alias("city"),
            col("shipping_address.state").alias("state")
        )
        
        flattened_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("json") \
            .option("compression", "gzip") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/json")
        
        print(f"✓ Data written to JSON format at {self.output_path}/json")
        self._display_file_stats(f"{self.output_path}/json")
    
    def read_and_query(self):
        """Demonstrate reading and querying row-oriented formats"""
        print("\n=== Reading Row-Oriented Formats ===")
        
        # Read Avro
        avro_df = self.spark.read.format("avro").load(f"{self.output_path}/avro")
        print("\nAvro Data Sample:")
        avro_df.show(5, truncate=False)
        
        # Query specific transactions (efficient for full row access)
        result = avro_df.filter(col("total_amount") > 5000) \
            .select("transaction_id", "customer_id", "total_amount", "category")
        
        print("\nHigh-value transactions:")
        result.show(10)
        
        return avro_df
    
    def _display_file_stats(self, path):
        """Display file size statistics"""
        import subprocess
        try:
            result = subprocess.run(['du', '-sh', path], capture_output=True, text=True)
            print(f"Storage size: {result.stdout.strip()}")
        except:
            print("Could not calculate file size")

# PATTERN 2: COLUMN-ORIENTED FORMAT PATTERN
# ============================================================================
# Use Case: OLAP workloads, analytical queries, column-specific aggregations
# Best for: Data warehousing, BI reporting, analytical queries

class ColumnOrientedFormatPattern:
    """
    Column-Oriented Format Pattern using Parquet
    
    Characteristics:
    - Stores data by columns
    - Excellent compression ratios
    - Efficient for analytical queries
    - Supports predicate pushdown
    - Column pruning optimization
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
        self.output_path = "/tmp/column_oriented_format"
    
    def write_parquet_format(self, df):
        """
        Write data in Parquet format (columnar)
        
        Benefits:
        - Excellent compression (especially for repeated values)
        - Fast column-based queries
        - Supports complex nested data
        - Industry standard for big data
        """
        print("\n=== Column-Oriented Format Pattern: Writing Parquet ===")
        
        # Write as Parquet with partitioning
        df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("parquet") \
            .option("compression", "snappy") \
            .partitionBy("category", "payment_method") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/parquet")
        
        print(f"✓ Data written to Parquet format at {self.output_path}/parquet")
        
        # Show partitioning structure
        self._show_partition_structure(f"{self.output_path}/parquet")
    
    def write_orc_format(self, df):
        """
        Write data in ORC format (columnar, optimized for Hive)
        
        Benefits:
        - Better compression than Parquet in some cases
        - Built-in indexes
        - ACID transaction support
        - Optimized for Hive workloads
        """
        print("\n=== Column-Oriented Format Pattern: Writing ORC ===")
        
        # Flatten for ORC (ORC handles nested data differently)
        flattened_df = df.select(
            "transaction_id",
            "customer_id",
            "product_id",
            "quantity",
            "unit_price",
            "total_amount",
            "transaction_date",
            "category",
            "payment_method",
            col("shipping_address.city").alias("city"),
            col("shipping_address.state").alias("state"),
            col("shipping_address.zip").alias("zip")
        )
        
        flattened_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("orc") \
            .option("compression", "zlib") \
            .partitionBy("category") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/orc")
        
        print(f"✓ Data written to ORC format at {self.output_path}/orc")
    
    def demonstrate_columnar_benefits(self):
        """
        Demonstrate the benefits of columnar storage for analytical queries
        """
        print("\n=== Demonstrating Columnar Format Benefits ===")
        
        # Read Parquet
        parquet_df = self.spark.read.parquet(f"{self.output_path}/parquet")
        
        # Analytical Query 1: Column aggregation (very efficient in columnar)
        print("\n1. Column Aggregation (Sum of total_amount by category):")
        category_sales = parquet_df.groupBy("category") \
            .agg(
                sum("total_amount").alias("total_sales"),
                avg("total_amount").alias("avg_transaction"),
                count("*").alias("transaction_count")
            ) \
            .orderBy(desc("total_sales"))
        
        category_sales.show()
        
        # Analytical Query 2: Selective column reading
        print("\n2. Selective Column Reading (only 3 columns):")
        selective_df = parquet_df.select("category", "total_amount", "transaction_date")
        print(f"Columns read: {selective_df.columns}")
        
        # Analytical Query 3: Predicate pushdown
        print("\n3. Predicate Pushdown (filter on partitioned column):")
        filtered_df = parquet_df.filter(
            (col("category") == "Electronics") & 
            (col("total_amount") > 1000)
        )
        print(f"Filtered records: {filtered_df.count()}")
        filtered_df.show(5)
        
        # Show query plan to demonstrate optimizations
        print("\n4. Query Execution Plan:")
        filtered_df.explain(True)
    
    def _show_partition_structure(self, path):
        """Display partition structure"""
        try:
            import subprocess
            result = subprocess.run(['find', path, '-type', 'd', '-maxdepth', 2], 
                                  capture_output=True, text=True)
            print("\nPartition structure:")
            print(result.stdout[:500])  # Show first 500 chars
        except:
            print("Could not display partition structure")


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 3: HYBRID FORMAT PATTERN
# ============================================================================
# Use Case: Mixed workloads, both OLTP and OLAP requirements
# Best for: Systems requiring both transactional and analytical capabilities

class HybridFormatPattern:
    """
    Hybrid Format Pattern combining row and columnar storage
    
    Characteristics:
    - Uses different formats for different access patterns
    - Hot data in row format, cold data in columnar
    - Optimizes for both read and write patterns
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
        self.output_path = "/tmp/hybrid_format"
    
    def implement_lambda_architecture(self, df):
        """
        Implement Lambda Architecture with hybrid storage
        
        Speed Layer: Row-oriented (Avro) for recent, frequently updated data
        Batch Layer: Column-oriented (Parquet) for historical, analytical data
        """
        print("\n=== Hybrid Format Pattern: Lambda Architecture ===")
        
        current_date = datetime.now()
        cutoff_date = current_date - timedelta(days=30)
        
        # Speed Layer: Recent data (last 30 days) in Avro
        speed_layer_df = df.filter(col("transaction_date") >= cutoff_date)
        speed_layer_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("avro") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/speed_layer")
        
        print(f"✓ Speed Layer: {speed_layer_df.count()} recent records in Avro format")
        
        # Batch Layer: Historical data in Parquet
        batch_layer_df = df.filter(col("transaction_date") < cutoff_date)
        batch_layer_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("parquet") \
            .partitionBy("category") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/batch_layer")
        
        print(f"✓ Batch Layer: {batch_layer_df.count()} historical records in Parquet format")
    
    def implement_hot_cold_storage(self, df):
        """
        Implement hot/cold storage pattern
        
        Hot Storage: Frequently accessed data in row format
        Cold Storage: Rarely accessed data in highly compressed columnar format
        """
        print("\n=== Hybrid Format Pattern: Hot/Cold Storage ===")
        
        # Identify hot data (high-value transactions)
        hot_data = df.filter(col("total_amount") > 1000)
        
        # Hot storage: Avro for fast access
        hot_data.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("avro") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/hot_storage")
        
        print(f"✓ Hot Storage: {hot_data.count()} high-value records in Avro")
        
        # Cold data (low-value transactions)
        cold_data = df.filter(col("total_amount") <= 1000)
        
        # Cold storage: Parquet with maximum compression
        cold_data.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("parquet") \
            .option("compression", "gzip") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/cold_storage")
        
        print(f"✓ Cold Storage: {cold_data.count()} standard records in compressed Parquet")
    
    def query_hybrid_storage(self):
        """Demonstrate querying across hybrid storage"""
        print("\n=== Querying Hybrid Storage ===")
        
        # Read from both layers
        speed_df = self.spark.read.format("avro") \
            .load(f"{self.output_path}/speed_layer")
        
        batch_df = self.spark.read.format("parquet") \
            .load(f"{self.output_path}/batch_layer")
        
        # Union for complete view
```python
        # Union for complete view
        complete_df = speed_df.union(batch_df)
        
        print(f"\nTotal records from hybrid storage: {complete_df.count()}")
        
        # Perform analytical query across both layers
        print("\nSales by category across all layers:")
        complete_df.groupBy("category") \
            .agg(
                sum("total_amount").alias("total_sales"),
                count("*").alias("transaction_count")
            ) \
            .orderBy(desc("total_sales")) \
            .show()
        
        return complete_df


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 4: NESTED FORMAT PATTERN
# ============================================================================
# Use Case: Complex hierarchical data, semi-structured data
# Best for: JSON-like data, document stores, complex relationships

class NestedFormatPattern:
    """
    Nested Format Pattern for handling complex hierarchical data
    
    Characteristics:
    - Preserves data hierarchy
    - Reduces joins
    - Efficient for document-oriented data
    - Supports schema evolution
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
        self.output_path = "/tmp/nested_format"
    
    def create_nested_schema(self):
        """Define complex nested schema"""
        return StructType([
            StructField("transaction_id", StringType(), False),
            StructField("customer", StructType([
                StructField("customer_id", StringType(), False),
                StructField("name", StringType(), True),
                StructField("email", StringType(), True),
                StructField("loyalty_tier", StringType(), True),
                StructField("preferences", MapType(StringType(), StringType()), True)
            ]), False),
            StructField("order", StructType([
                StructField("order_date", TimestampType(), False),
                StructField("items", ArrayType(StructType([
                    StructField("product_id", StringType(), False),
                    StructField("product_name", StringType(), False),
                    StructField("quantity", IntegerType(), False),
                    StructField("unit_price", DoubleType(), False),
                    StructField("discount", DoubleType(), True),
                    StructField("attributes", MapType(StringType(), StringType()), True)
                ])), False),
                StructField("shipping", StructType([
                    StructField("address", StructType([
                        StructField("street", StringType(), True),
                        StructField("city", StringType(), True),
                        StructField("state", StringType(), True),
                        StructField("zip", StringType(), True),
                        StructField("country", StringType(), True)
                    ]), True),
                    StructField("method", StringType(), True),
                    StructField("tracking_number", StringType(), True)
                ]), True),
                StructField("payment", StructType([
                    StructField("method", StringType(), False),
                    StructField("card_last_four", StringType(), True),
                    StructField("transaction_fee", DoubleType(), True)
                ]), False)
            ]), False),
            StructField("metadata", StructType([
                StructField("source_system", StringType(), True),
                StructField("created_at", TimestampType(), True),
                StructField("updated_at", TimestampType(), True),
                StructField("version", IntegerType(), True)
            ]), True)
        ])
    
    def create_nested_data(self):
        """Create sample nested data"""
        nested_data = []
        
        for i in range(1000):
            items = []
            for j in range(random.randint(1, 5)):
                items.append({
                    "product_id": f"PROD{random.randint(1, 500):04d}",
                    "product_name": f"Product {j}",
                    "quantity": random.randint(1, 10),
                    "unit_price": round(random.uniform(10, 500), 2),
                    "discount": round(random.uniform(0, 0.3), 2),
                    "attributes": {
                        "color": random.choice(["Red", "Blue", "Green"]),
                        "size": random.choice(["S", "M", "L", "XL"])
                    }
                })
            
            nested_data.append({
                "transaction_id": f"TXN{i:06d}",
                "customer": {
                    "customer_id": f"CUST{random.randint(1, 500):04d}",
                    "name": f"Customer {i}",
                    "email": f"customer{i}@example.com",
                    "loyalty_tier": random.choice(["Bronze", "Silver", "Gold", "Platinum"]),
                    "preferences": {
                        "newsletter": "true",
                        "notifications": "email"
                    }
                },
                "order": {
                    "order_date": datetime.now() - timedelta(days=random.randint(0, 365)),
                    "items": items,
                    "shipping": {
                        "address": {
                            "street": f"{random.randint(1, 999)} Main St",
                            "city": random.choice(["New York", "Los Angeles", "Chicago"]),
                            "state": random.choice(["NY", "CA", "IL"]),
                            "zip": f"{random.randint(10000, 99999)}",
                            "country": "USA"
                        },
                        "method": random.choice(["Standard", "Express", "Overnight"]),
                        "tracking_number": f"TRK{random.randint(100000, 999999)}"
                    },
                    "payment": {
                        "method": random.choice(["Credit Card", "Debit Card", "PayPal"]),
                        "card_last_four": f"{random.randint(1000, 9999)}",
                        "transaction_fee": round(random.uniform(0.5, 5.0), 2)
                    }
                },
                "metadata": {
                    "source_system": "POS",
                    "created_at": datetime.now(),
                    "updated_at": datetime.now(),
                    "version": 1
                }
            })
        
        return nested_data
    
    def write_nested_parquet(self, df):
        """
        Write nested data in Parquet format
        
        Benefits:
        - Preserves nested structure
        - Efficient storage of complex types
        - Supports schema evolution
        - Column pruning works on nested fields
        """
        print("\n=== Nested Format Pattern: Writing Nested Parquet ===")
        
        df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("parquet") \
            .option("compression", "snappy") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/nested_parquet")
        
        print(f"✓ Nested data written to Parquet")
        
        # Show schema
        print("\nNested Schema:")
        df.printSchema()
    
    def write_nested_avro(self, df):
        """
        Write nested data in Avro format
        
        Benefits:
        - Excellent support for complex types
        - Schema evolution
        - Compact representation
        """
        print("\n=== Nested Format Pattern: Writing Nested Avro ===")
        
        df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("avro") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/nested_avro")
        
        print(f"✓ Nested data written to Avro")
    
    def query_nested_data(self):
        """Demonstrate querying nested data structures"""
        print("\n=== Querying Nested Data ===")
        
        # Read nested Parquet
        nested_df = self.spark.read.parquet(f"{self.output_path}/nested_parquet")
        
        # Query 1: Access nested fields directly
        print("\n1. Accessing Nested Fields:")
        nested_df.select(
            "transaction_id",
            "customer.customer_id",
            "customer.name",
            "customer.loyalty_tier",
            "order.payment.method"
        ).show(5, truncate=False)
        
        # Query 2: Explode array of items
        print("\n2. Exploding Nested Arrays:")
        exploded_df = nested_df.select(
            "transaction_id",
            "customer.customer_id",
            explode("order.items").alias("item")
        ).select(
            "transaction_id",
            "customer_id",
            "item.product_id",
            "item.product_name",
            "item.quantity",
            "item.unit_price"
        )
        exploded_df.show(10, truncate=False)
        
        # Query 3: Aggregate on nested data
        print("\n3. Aggregating Nested Data:")
        nested_df.select(
            "customer.loyalty_tier",
            explode("order.items").alias("item")
        ).groupBy("loyalty_tier") \
         .agg(
             sum(col("item.quantity") * col("item.unit_price")).alias("total_revenue"),
             count("*").alias("items_sold")
         ) \
         .orderBy(desc("total_revenue")) \
         .show()
        
        # Query 4: Filter on nested fields
        print("\n4. Filtering on Nested Fields:")
        high_value_customers = nested_df.filter(
            col("customer.loyalty_tier") == "Platinum"
        ).select(
            "transaction_id",
            "customer.name",
            "customer.email",
            "order.shipping.address.city"
        )
        high_value_customers.show(5, truncate=False)
        
        # Query 5: Access map type fields
        print("\n5. Accessing Map Type Fields:")
        nested_df.select(
            "transaction_id",
            "customer.preferences.newsletter",
            col("customer.preferences")["notifications"].alias("notification_pref")
        ).show(5, truncate=False)
        
        return nested_df
    
    def flatten_nested_structure(self, df):
        """
        Demonstrate flattening nested structures when needed
        """
        print("\n=== Flattening Nested Structure ===")
        
        # Flatten the nested structure
        flattened_df = df.select(
            "transaction_id",
            col("customer.customer_id").alias("customer_id"),
            col("customer.name").alias("customer_name"),
            col("customer.loyalty_tier").alias("loyalty_tier"),
            col("order.order_date").alias("order_date"),
            col("order.payment.method").alias("payment_method"),
            col("order.shipping.address.city").alias("shipping_city"),
            col("order.shipping.address.state").alias("shipping_state"),
            col("order.shipping.method").alias("shipping_method")
        )
        
        print("Flattened Schema:")
        flattened_df.printSchema()
        
        flattened_df.show(5, truncate=False)
        
        # Write flattened version
        flattened_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("parquet") \
            .partitionBy("shipping_state") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/flattened_parquet")
        
        print("✓ Flattened data written")


# ============================================================================
# PATTERN 5: SELF-DESCRIBING FORMAT PATTERN
# ============================================================================
# Use Case: Schema evolution, data sharing, long-term archival
# Best for: Data lakes, schema-on-read scenarios, data exchange

class SelfDescribingFormatPattern:
    """
    Self-Describing Format Pattern with embedded schema
    
    Characteristics:
    - Schema embedded in data files
    - No external schema registry needed
    - Supports schema evolution
    - Self-contained and portable
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
        self.output_path = "/tmp/self_describing_format"
    
    def write_avro_with_schema(self, df):
        """
        Write Avro with embedded schema
        
        Benefits:
        - Schema is part of the file
        - Readers can discover schema automatically
        - Schema evolution support
        - Version compatibility
        """
        print("\n=== Self-Describing Format Pattern: Avro ===")
        
        # Write Avro (schema is automatically embedded)
        df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("avro") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/avro_self_describing")
        
        print("✓ Avro written with embedded schema")
        
        # Read back and show schema
        avro_df = self.spark.read.format("avro") \
            .load(f"{self.output_path}/avro_self_describing")
        
        print("\nSchema automatically discovered from Avro:")
        avro_df.printSchema()
    
    def write_parquet_with_metadata(self, df):
        """
        Write Parquet with metadata
        
        Benefits:
        - Schema in file footer
        - Column statistics embedded
        - Efficient for analytical queries
        """
        print("\n=== Self-Describing Format Pattern: Parquet ===")
        
        # Add custom metadata
        df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("parquet") \
            .option("compression", "snappy") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/parquet_self_describing")
        
        print("✓ Parquet written with embedded schema and metadata")
        
        # Read and show schema
        parquet_df = self.spark.read.parquet(f"{self.output_path}/parquet_self_describing")
        print("\nSchema from Parquet footer:")
        parquet_df.printSchema()
    
    def demonstrate_schema_evolution(self, df):

        """
        print("\n=== Demonstrating Schema Evolution ===")
        
        # Version 1: Original schema

            .format("avro") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/schema_evolution/v1")

                  .withColumn("promotion_code", lit(None).cast(StringType())) \
                  .withColumn("referral_source", lit("Direct"))
        
        df_v2.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("avro") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/schema_evolution/v2")
        
        # Version 3: Rename and remove columns
        print("\n3. Writing Version 3 (Modified Schema):")
        df_v3 = df.withColumnRenamed("total_amount", "order_total") \
                  .withColumn("discount_applied", lit(0.0)) \
                  .drop("payment_method")
        
        df_v3.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("avro") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/schema_evolution/v3")
        
        # Read all versions
        print("\n4. Reading All Versions:")
        
        v1 = self.spark.read.format("avro") \
            .load(f
```python
            .load(f"{self.output_path}/schema_evolution/v1")
        print("\nVersion 1 Schema:")
        v1.printSchema()
        print(f"Columns: {v1.columns}")
        
        v2 = self.spark.read.format("avro") \
            .load(f"{self.output_path}/schema_evolution/v2")
        print("\nVersion 2 Schema:")
        v2.printSchema()
        print(f"Columns: {v2.columns}")
        
        v3 = self.spark.read.format("avro") \
            .load(f"{self.output_path}/schema_evolution/v3")
        print("\nVersion 3 Schema:")
        v3.printSchema()
        print(f"Columns: {v3.columns}")
        
        # Demonstrate backward compatibility
        print("\n5. Reading with Schema Compatibility:")
        try:
            # Read all versions together (Avro handles schema evolution)
            all_versions = self.spark.read.format("avro").load(
                f"{self.output_path}/schema_evolution/*"
            )
            print(f"✓ Successfully read all versions together")
            print(f"Total records: {all_versions.count()}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"✗ Error reading multiple versions: {e}")
    
    def write_with_schema_registry_pattern(self, df):
        """
        Simulate schema registry pattern for self-describing data
        """
        print("\n=== Schema Registry Pattern ===")
        
        # Extract and save schema separately
        schema_json = df.schema.json()
        
        # Save schema to a separate location (simulating schema registry)
        schema_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(
            [(1, schema_json, datetime.now(), "v1.0")],
            ["schema_id", "schema_definition", "created_at", "version"]
        )
        
        schema_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("parquet") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/schema_registry")
        
        print("✓ Schema saved to registry")
        
        # Write data with schema reference
        df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("parquet") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/data_with_schema_ref")
        
        print("✓ Data written with schema reference")
        
        # Read schema from registry
        print("\nReading schema from registry:")
        schema_registry = self.spark.read.parquet(f"{self.output_path}/schema_registry")
        schema_registry.show(truncate=False)
    
    def create_self_describing_json(self, df):
        """
        Create self-describing JSON with embedded metadata
        """
        print("\n=== Self-Describing JSON ===")
        
        # Add metadata to each record
        metadata_df = df.withColumn("_metadata", 
            struct(
                lit("transaction_system").alias("source"),
                current_timestamp().alias("ingestion_time"),
                lit("1.0").alias("schema_version"),
                lit("production").alias("environment")
            )
        )
        
        metadata_df.write \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .format("json") \
            .save(f"{self.output_path}/self_describing_json")
        
        print("✓ Self-describing JSON written with metadata")
        
        # Read and display
        json_df = self.spark.read.json(f"{self.output_path}/self_describing_json")
        print("\nSample with embedded metadata:")
        json_df.select("transaction_id", "_metadata").show(3, truncate=False)


# ============================================================================
# PERFORMANCE COMPARISON AND BENCHMARKING
# ============================================================================

class FormatPerformanceComparison:
    """
    Compare performance characteristics of different storage formats
    """
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
        self.output_path = "/tmp/format_comparison"
    
    def benchmark_write_performance(self, df):
        """Benchmark write performance for different formats"""
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("WRITE PERFORMANCE COMPARISON")
        print("="*70)
        
        formats = {
            'parquet': {'compression': 'snappy'},
            'orc': {'compression': 'zlib'},
            'avro': {'compression': 'snappy'},
            'json': {'compression': 'gzip'}
        }
        
        results = []
        
        for format_name, options in formats.items():
            print(f"\nTesting {format_name.upper()} write...")
            start_time = datetime.now()
            
            writer = df.write.mode("overwrite").format(format_name)
            for key, value in options.items():
                writer = writer.option(key, value)
            
            writer.save(f"{self.output_path}/benchmark_{format_name}")
            
            end_time = datetime.now()
            duration = (end_time - start_time).total_seconds()
            
            # Get file size
            import subprocess
            try:
                result = subprocess.run(
                    ['du', '-sb', f"{self.output_path}/benchmark_{format_name}"],
                    capture_output=True, text=True
                )
                size_bytes = int(result.stdout.split()[0])
                size_mb = size_bytes / (1024 * 1024)
            except:
                size_mb = 0
            
            results.append({
                'format': format_name,
                'write_time_sec': round(duration, 2),
                'size_mb': round(size_mb, 2),
                'compression': options.get('compression', 'none')
            })
            
            print(f"✓ {format_name}: {duration:.2f}s, {size_mb:.2f} MB")
        
        # Display results
        results_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(results)
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("WRITE PERFORMANCE SUMMARY")
        print("="*70)
        results_df.orderBy("write_time_sec").show(truncate=False)
        
        return results_df
    
    def benchmark_read_performance(self):
        """Benchmark read performance for different formats"""
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("READ PERFORMANCE COMPARISON")
        print("="*70)
        
        formats = ['parquet', 'orc', 'avro', 'json']
        results = []
        
        for format_name in formats:
            print(f"\nTesting {format_name.upper()} read...")
            
            # Full scan
            start_time = datetime.now()
            df = self.spark.read.format(format_name) \
                .load(f"{self.output_path}/benchmark_{format_name}")
            count = df.count()
            end_time = datetime.now()
            full_scan_time = (end_time - start_time).total_seconds()
            
            # Column projection
            start_time = datetime.now()
            df_projected = self.spark.read.format(format_name) \
                .load(f"{self.output_path}/benchmark_{format_name}") \
                .select("transaction_id", "total_amount", "category")
            count_projected = df_projected.count()
            end_time = datetime.now()
            projection_time = (end_time - start_time).total_seconds()
            
            # Predicate pushdown
            start_time = datetime.now()
            df_filtered = self.spark.read.format(format_name) \
                .load(f"{self.output_path}/benchmark_{format_name}") \
                .filter(col("total_amount") > 1000)
            count_filtered = df_filtered.count()
            end_time = datetime.now()
            filter_time = (end_time - start_time).total_seconds()
            
            results.append({
                'format': format_name,
                'full_scan_sec': round(full_scan_time, 2),
                'column_projection_sec': round(projection_time, 2),
                'predicate_pushdown_sec': round(filter_time, 2),
                'records': count
            })
            
            print(f"✓ {format_name}: Full={full_scan_time:.2f}s, " +
                  f"Projection={projection_time:.2f}s, Filter={filter_time:.2f}s")
        
        # Display results
        results_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(results)
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("READ PERFORMANCE SUMMARY")
        print("="*70)
        results_df.show(truncate=False)
        
        return results_df
    
    def analyze_compression_ratios(self):
        """Analyze compression effectiveness for different formats"""
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("COMPRESSION RATIO ANALYSIS")
        print("="*70)
        
        formats = ['parquet', 'orc', 'avro', 'json']
        results = []
        
        import subprocess
        
        for format_name in formats:
            path = f"{self.output_path}/benchmark_{format_name}"
            
            try:
                # Get compressed size
                result = subprocess.run(
                    ['du', '-sb', path],
                    capture_output=True, text=True
                )
                compressed_size = int(result.stdout.split()[0])
                
                # Read data to estimate uncompressed size
                df = self.spark.read.format(format_name).load(path)
                
                # Estimate uncompressed size (rough approximation)
                # Based on average row size * number of rows
                sample_size = df.limit(100).toJSON().map(lambda x: len(x)).sum()
                avg_row_size = sample_size / 100
                total_rows = df.count()
                estimated_uncompressed = avg_row_size * total_rows
                
                compression_ratio = estimated_uncompressed / compressed_size if compressed_size > 0 else 0
                
                results.append({
                    'format': format_name,
                    'compressed_mb': round(compressed_size / (1024*1024), 2),
                    'estimated_uncompressed_mb': round(estimated_uncompressed / (1024*1024), 2),
                    'compression_ratio': round(compression_ratio, 2),
                    'space_saved_pct': round((1 - 1/compression_ratio) * 100, 2) if compression_ratio > 0 else 0
                })
                
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Error analyzing {format_name}: {e}")
        
        results_df = self.spark.createDataFrame(results)
        results_df.orderBy(desc("compression_ratio")).show(truncate=False)
        
        return results_df

        # 5. Repartitioning

def cleanup_demo_files():
    """Clean up demonstration files"""
    import shutil
    import os
    
    paths = [
        "/tmp/row_oriented_format",
        "/tmp/column_oriented_format",
        "/tmp/hybrid_format",
        "/tmp/nested_format",
        "/tmp/self_describing_format",
        "/tmp/format_comparison"
    ]
    
    print("\n🧹 Cleaning up demonstration files...")
    for path in paths:
        if os.path.exists(path):
            try:
                shutil.rmtree(path)
                print(f"✓ Removed {path}")
            except Exception as e:
                print(f"✗ Error removing {path}: {e}")

class TroubleshootingGuide:
    """Common issues and solutions for storage formats"""
    
    @staticmethod
    def print_troubleshooting_guide():
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE")
        print("="*70)
        
        guide = """
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    COMMON ISSUES AND SOLUTIONS                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                      │
│ ISSUE 1: Schema Mismatch Errors                                     │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
│ Symptom: "Schema mismatch" when reading Parquet files               │
│                                                                      │
│ Solutions:                                                           │
│ • Enable schema merging:                                             │
│   spark.read.option("mergeSchema", "true").parquet(path)             │
│                                                                      │
│ • Use Avro for better schema evolution                               │
│                                                                      │
│ • Implement schema validation before writing                         │
│                                                                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ISSUE 2: Small Files Problem                                        │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
│ Symptom: Too many small files, slow queries                          │
│                                                                      │
│ Solutions:                                                           │
│ • Coalesce before writing:                                           │
│   df.coalesce(10).write.parquet(path)                                │
│                                                                      │
│ • Repartition based on data size:                                    │
│   df.repartition(num_partitions).write.parquet(path)                 │
│                                                                      │
│ • Use compaction jobs periodically                                   │
│                                                                      │
│ • Configure file size targets:                                       │
│   spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.maxRecordsPerFile", 1000000)      │
│                                                                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ISSUE 3: Out of Memory Errors                                       │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
│ Symptom: OOM when reading large files                                │
│                                                                      │
│ Solutions:                                                           │
│ • Increase executor memory                                           │
│                                                                      │
│ • Use column pruning:                                                │
│   df.select("col1", "col2").filter(...)                              │
│                                                                      │
│ • Enable adaptive query execution:                                   │
│   spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")              │
│                                                                      │
│ • Process data in batches                                            │
│                                                                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ISSUE 4: Slow Write Performance                                     │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
│ Symptom: Write operations taking too long                            │
│                                                                      │
│ Solutions:                                                           │
│ • Reduce partitioning depth (avoid over-partitioning)                │
│                                                                      │
│ • Use faster compression (snappy instead of gzip)                    │
│                                                                      │
│ • Increase parallelism:                                              │
│   df.repartition(200).write.parquet(path)                            │
│                                                                      │
│ • Disable compression for very fast writes:                          │
│   .option("compression", "none")                                     │
│                                                                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ISSUE 5: Corrupted Files                                            │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
│ Symptom: Cannot read files, corruption errors                        │
│                                                                      │
│ Solutions:                                                           │
│ • Enable ignore corrupt files:                                       │
│   spark.conf.set("spark.sql.files.ignoreCorruptFiles", "true")      │
│                                                                      │
│ • Use checksums for validation                                       │
│                                                                      │
│ • Implement retry logic for writes                                   │
│                                                                      │
│ • Use transactional writes (Delta Lake, Iceberg)                     │
│                                                                      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ISSUE 6: Partition Pruning Not Working                              │
│ ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────   │
│ Symptom: All partitions scanned despite filter                       │
│                                                                      │
│ Solutions:                                                           │
│ • Ensure filter is on partition column                               │
│                                                                      │
│ • Check partition column data types match                            │
│                                                                      │
│ • Verify partition discovery:                                        │
│   spark.read.option("basePath", path).parquet(path)                  │
│                                                                      │
│ • Use explicit partition filters:                                    │
│   df.filter(col("partition_col") == value)                           │
│                                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PERFORMANCE DEBUGGING                             │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                      │
│ 1. Check Query Plan:                                                 │
│    df.explain
```python
│    df.explain(True)  # Shows physical and logical plans                │
│                                                                      │
│ 2. Monitor File Statistics:                                         │
│    spark.read.parquet(path).rdd.getNumPartitions()                   │
│                                                                      │
│ 3. Check Compression Effectiveness:                                 │
│    # Compare file sizes with different compression                   │
│                                                                      │
│ 4. Profile Memory Usage:                                            │
│    # Use Spark UI to monitor executor memory                         │
│                                                                      │
│ 5. Analyze Partition Skew:                                          │
│    df.groupBy("partition_col").count().show()                        │
│                                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
        """
        print(guide)

# MIGRATION STRATEGIES
# ============================================================================

class FormatMigrationStrategies:
    """Strategies for migrating between storage formats"""
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def migrate_json_to_parquet(self, source_path, target_path):
        """Migrate from JSON to Parquet"""
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("MIGRATION: JSON → PARQUET")
        print("="*70)
        
        print("\nStep 1: Reading JSON data...")
        json_df = self.spark.read.json(source_path)
        
        print(f"Records to migrate: {json_df.count()}")
        print("\nOriginal Schema:")
        json_df.printSchema()
        
        print("\nStep 2: Optimizing schema...")
        # Infer better data types if needed
        optimized_df = json_df
        
        print("\nStep 3: Writing to Parquet with partitioning...")
        optimized_df.write \
            .format("parquet") \
            .option("compression", "snappy") \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .save(target_path)
        
        print("✓ Migration complete!")
        
        # Validate migration
        print("\nStep 4: Validating migration...")
        parquet_df = self.spark.read.parquet(target_path)
        
        json_count = json_df.count()
        parquet_count = parquet_df.count()
        
        print(f"JSON records: {json_count}")
        print(f"Parquet records: {parquet_count}")
        print(f"Match: {'✓' if json_count == parquet_count else '✗'}")
        
        return parquet_df
    
    def migrate_avro_to_parquet_with_partitioning(self, source_path, target_path, partition_cols):
        """Migrate from Avro to partitioned Parquet"""
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("MIGRATION: AVRO → PARTITIONED PARQUET")
        print("="*70)
        
        print("\nStep 1: Reading Avro data...")
        avro_df = self.spark.read.format("avro").load(source_path)
        
        print(f"Records to migrate: {avro_df.count()}")
        
        print(f"\nStep 2: Writing to Parquet with partitioning by {partition_cols}...")
        avro_df.write \
            .format("parquet") \
            .option("compression", "snappy") \
            .partitionBy(*partition_cols) \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .save(target_path)
        
        print("✓ Migration complete with partitioning!")
        
        # Show partition structure
        print("\nPartition structure created:")
        parquet_df = self.spark.read.parquet(target_path)
        parquet_df.select(*partition_cols).distinct().show(10)
        
        return parquet_df
    
    def incremental_migration_pattern(self, source_path, target_path, checkpoint_col):
        """Demonstrate incremental migration pattern"""
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("INCREMENTAL MIGRATION PATTERN")
        print("="*70)
        
        migration_guide = f"""
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    INCREMENTAL MIGRATION STRATEGY                    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                      │
│ 1. DUAL-WRITE PHASE                                                 │
│    • Write to both old and new formats simultaneously               │
│    • Duration: 1-2 weeks                                            │
│    • Validate data consistency                                      │
│                                                                      │
│ 2. BACKFILL HISTORICAL DATA                                         │
│    • Migrate old data in batches                                    │
│    • Use checkpoint column: {checkpoint_col}                        │
│    • Monitor progress and validate                                  │
│                                                                      │
│ 3. CUTOVER READS                                                     │
│    • Gradually shift reads to new format                            │
│    • Monitor performance metrics                                    │
│    • Keep old format as backup                                      │
│                                                                      │
│ 4. DEPRECATE OLD FORMAT                                             │
│    • After validation period (2-4 weeks)                            │
│    • Archive old data                                               │
│    • Clean up old storage                                           │
│                                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

IMPLEMENTATION EXAMPLE:

# Phase 1: Dual Write
def dual_write(df, old_path, new_path):
    # Write to old format
    df.write.format("json").mode("append").save(old_path)
    
    # Write to new format
    df.write.format("parquet") \\
        .partitionBy("date") \\
        .mode("append") \\
        .save(new_path)

# Phase 2: Backfill with checkpointing
def backfill_batch(checkpoint_value):
    old_df = spark.read.json(old_path) \\
        .filter(col("{checkpoint_col}") > checkpoint_value)
    
    old_df.write.format("parquet") \\
        .mode("append") \\
        .save(new_path)
    
    return old_df.agg(max("{checkpoint_col}")).collect()[0][0]

# Phase 3: Gradual cutover
def read_with_fallback(path_new, path_old, date):
    try:
        return spark.read.parquet(path_new) \\
            .filter(col("date") == date)
    except:
        return spark.read.json(path_old) \\
            .filter(col("date") == date)
        """
        print(migration_guide)

# ADVANCED OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES

class AdvancedOptimizations:
    """Advanced optimization techniques for storage formats"""
    
    def __init__(self, spark_session):
        self.spark = spark_session
    
    def demonstrate_z_ordering(self, df, output_path):
        """Demonstrate Z-ordering for better data locality"""
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("ADVANCED OPTIMIZATION: Z-ORDERING")
        print("="*70)
        
        print("""
Z-Ordering (also called multi-dimensional clustering):
- Colocates related data in the same files
- Improves query performance for multiple filter columns
- Reduces data scanning

Example use case:
- Frequently filter by customer_id AND product_category
- Z-ordering ensures these combinations are stored together
        """)
        
        # Note: Z-ordering is typically available in Delta Lake
        # Here we demonstrate the concept with sorting
        
        print("\nSimulating Z-ordering with sorting...")
        from pyspark.sql.functions import col
        
        # Sort by multiple columns to achieve similar effect
        optimized_df = df.repartition(10, "category", "customer_id") \
            .sortWithinPartitions("category", "customer_id")
        
        optimized_df.write \
            .format("parquet") \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .save(output_path)
        
        print("✓ Data written with optimized layout")
    
    def demonstrate_bucketing(self, df, output_path):
        """Demonstrate bucketing for join optimization"""
        print("\n" + "="*70)
        print("ADVANCED OPTIMIZATION: BUCKETING")
        print("="*70)
        
        print("""
Bucketing:
- Pre-shuffles data into buckets based on column values
- Eliminates shuffle during joins on bucketed column
- Significant performance improvement for repeated joins

Best for:
- Tables frequently joined on the same column
- Large fact tables in star schema
        """)
        
        print("\nCreating bucketed table...")
        
        df.write \
            .format("parquet") \
            .bucketBy(50, "customer_id") \
            .sortBy("transaction_date") \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .saveAsTable("bucketed_transactions")
        
        print("✓ Bucketed table created")
        print("  - 50 buckets on customer_id")
        print("  - Sorted by transaction_date within buckets")

        guide = """

│                        BLOOM FILTER INDEXES                          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                                      │
│ What are Bloom Filters?                                             │
│ • Probabilistic data structure                                      │
│ • Quickly test if element is in set                                 │
│ • Can have false positives, never false negatives                   │
│                                                                      │
│ Benefits for Storage:                                               │
│ • Skip reading files that definitely don't contain value            │
│ • Reduce I/O for highly selective queries                           │
│ • Especially useful for high-cardinality columns                    │
│                                                                      │
│ Use Cases:                                                           │
│ • Point lookups (WHERE id = '12345')                                │
│ • IN clauses with many values                                       │
│ • Join optimization                                                  │
│                                                                      │
│ Available in:                                                        │
│ • Delta Lake (native support)                                       │
│ • ORC (built-in bloom filters)                                      │
│ • Parquet (via custom implementations)                              │
│                                                                      │
│ Example (Delta Lake):                                               │
│                                                                      │

│       transaction_id STRING,                                        │
│       customer_id STRING,                                           │
│       amount DECIMAL(10,2)                                          │

Calculation:
        """)

        df.cache()
        total_size_mb = df.count() * 0.001  # Rough estimate
        optimal_file_size_mb = 256
        optimal_num_files = max(1, int(total_size_mb / optimal_file_size_mb))
        
        print(f"Estimated data size: {total_size_mb:.2f} MB")
        print(f"Target file size: {optimal_file_size_mb} MB")
        print(f"Optimal number of files: {optimal_num_files}")
        
        print(f"\nRepartitioning to {optimal_num_files} partitions...")
        df.repartition(optimal_num_files).write \
            .format("parquet") \
            .mode("overwrite") \
            .save(output_path)
        
        print("✓ Data written with optimized file sizes")

def compare_formats_side_by_side(spark, df):
    """Side-by-side comparison of all formats"""
    print("\n" + "="*70)
    print("SIDE-BY-SIDE FORMAT COMPARISON")
    print("="*70)
    
    import time
    import subprocess
    
    formats = ['parquet', 'orc', 'avro', 'json']
    results = []
    
    for fmt in formats:
        path = f"/tmp/comparison_{fmt}"
        
        # Write test
        start = time.time()
        df.write.format(fmt).mode("overwrite").save(path)
        write_time = time.time() - start
        
        # Read test
        start = time.time()
        read_df = spark.read.format(fmt).load(path)
        count = read_df.count()
        read_time = time.time() - start
        
        # Size test
        try:
            result = subprocess.run(['du', '-sb', path], 
                                  capture_output=True, text=True)
            size_bytes = int(result.stdout.split()[0])
            size_mb = size_bytes / (1024 * 1024)
        except:
            size_mb = 0
        
        results.append({
            'format': fmt,
            'write_sec': round(write_time, 3),
            'read_sec': round(read_time, 3),
            'size_mb': round(size_mb, 2),
            'records': count
        })
    
    # Display results
    results_df = spark.createDataFrame(results)
    print("\nComparison Results:")
    results_df.show(truncate=False)
    
    # Calculate winners
    write_winner = min(results, key=lambda x: x['write_sec'])
    read_winner = min(results, key=lambda x: x['read_sec'])
    size_winner = min(results, key=lambda x: x['size_mb'])
    
    print("\n🏆 Winners:")
    print(f"  Fastest Write:  {write_winner['format'].upper()} ({write_winner['write_sec']}s)")
    print(f"  Fastest Read:   {read_winner['format'].upper()} ({read_winner['read_sec']}s)")
    print(f"  Smallest Size:  {size_winner['format'].upper()} ({size_winner['size_mb']} MB)")

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import *

    .appName("StreamingIngestion") \\

# Define schema

    StructField("event_id", StringType(), False),
    StructField("user_id", StringType(), False),

    StructField("timestamp", TimestampType(), False),
    StructField("properties", MapType(StringType(), StringType()), True)
])

    .option("subscribe", "events") \\
    .load() \\
    .select(from_json(col("value").cast("string"), schema).alias("data")) \\
    .select("data.*")

# Write stream to Avro
query = streaming_df.writeStream \\
    .format("avro") \\
    .option("path", "/data/streaming/events") \\
    .option("checkpointLocation", "/checkpoints/events") \\
    .outputMode("append") \\
    .start()

query.awaitTermination()

TEMPLATE 3: Data Lake Medallion Architecture
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import *

spark = SparkSession.builder \\
    .appName("MedallionArchitecture") \\
    .getOrCreate()

# BRONZE LAYER: Raw data ingestion
def ingest_to_bronze(source_path, bronze_path):
    raw_df = spark.read \\
        .format("json") \\
        .load(source_path) \\
        .withColumn("ingestion_timestamp", current_timestamp()) \\
        .withColumn("source_file", input_file_name())
    
    raw_df.write \\
        .format("avro") \\
        .partitionBy("ingestion_date") \\
        .mode("append") \\
        .save(bronze_path)
    
    return raw_df

# SILVER LAYER: Cleaned and validated
def process_to_silver(bronze_path, silver_path):
    bronze_df = spark.read.format("avro").load(bronze_path)
    
    silver_df = bronze_df \\
        .dropDuplicates(["id"]) \\
        .filter(col("amount").isNotNull()) \\
        .withColumn("processed_timestamp", current_timestamp())
    
    silver_df.write \\
        .format("parquet") \\
        .option("compression", "snappy") \\
        .partitionBy("business_date") \\
        .mode("overwrite") \\
        .save(silver_path)
    
    return silver_df

# GOLD LAYER: Business aggregates
def aggregate_to_gold(silver_path, gold_path):
    silver_df = spark.read.parquet(silver_path)
    
    gold_df = silver_df \\
        .groupBy("category", "business_date") \\
        .agg(
            sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
            count("*").alias("transaction_count"),
            avg("amount").alias("avg_amount")
        )
    
    gold_df.write \\
        .format("parquet") \\
        .option("compression", "zstd") \\
        .partitionBy("business_date") \\
        .mode("overwrite") \\
        .save(gold_path)
    
    return gold_df

# Execute pipeline
bronze_df = ingest_to_bronze("/source/raw", "/lake/bronze")
silver_df = process_to_silver("/lake/bronze", "/lake/silver")
gold_df = aggregate_to_gold("/lake/silver", "/lake/gold")

print("✓ Medallion pipeline completed")

from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import *
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

spark = SparkSession.builder \\
    .appName("IncrementalProcessing") \\
    .getOrCreate()

def process_incremental(source_path, target_path, checkpoint_path):
    # Read checkpoint (last processed timestamp)
    try:
        checkpoint_df = spark.read.parquet(checkpoint_path)
        last_timestamp = checkpoint_df.agg(max("max_timestamp")).collect()[0][0]
    except:
        last_timestamp = datetime(2020, 1, 1)
    
    print(f"Processing data after: {last_timestamp}")
    
    # Read incremental data
    incremental_df = spark.read.parquet(source_path) \\
        .filter(col("timestamp") > last_timestamp)
    
    if incremental_df.count() == 0:
        print("No new data to process")
        return
    
    # Process data
    processed_df = incremental_df \\
        .withColumn("processed_date", current_date())
    
    # Write processed data
    processed_df.write \\
        .format("parquet") \\
        .partitionBy("processed_date") \\
        .mode("append") \\
        .save(target_path)
    
    # Update checkpoint
    new_checkpoint = spark.createDataFrame(
        [(incremental_df.agg(max("timestamp")).collect()[0][0],)],
        ["max_timestamp"]
    )
    new_checkpoint.write.mode("overwrite").parquet(checkpoint_path)
    
    print(f"✓ Processed {incremental_df.count()} new records")

# Run incremental processing
process_incremental(
    "/data/source",
    "/data/processed",
    "/checkpoints/last_run"
)
