## Best Practices and Guidelines Documentation

```python
"""
Best Practices and Guidelines for Resource Pool Patterns
"""

class ResourcePoolBestPractices:
    """
    Collection of best practices for implementing and using resource pool patterns.
    """
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_pattern_selection_guide() -> str:
        """
        Guide for selecting the appropriate resource pool pattern.
        
        Returns:
            Formatted guide text
        """
        guide = """
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        RESOURCE POOL PATTERN SELECTION GUIDE
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        
        1. STATIC RESOURCE POOL
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ✓ Use When:
          • Workload is predictable and consistent
          • Resources requirements are well-known
          • Running scheduled batch jobs
          • Cost predictability is important
          • Simple resource management is preferred
        
        ✗ Avoid When:
          • Workload varies significantly
          • Need to optimize resource utilization
          • Processing ad-hoc queries
          • Cost optimization is critical
        
        📊 Example Use Cases:
          • Daily ETL pipelines
          • Monthly reporting jobs
          • Scheduled data exports
          • Regular model training
        
        ⚙️ Configuration Tips:
          • Set executor count based on average workload
          • Allocate 20% buffer for peak times
          • Use consistent executor sizes
          • Monitor and adjust quarterly
        
        
        2. DYNAMIC RESOURCE POOL
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ✓ Use When:
          • Workload varies throughout the day
          • Processing different data sizes
          • Need automatic resource scaling
          • Want to balance cost and performance
        
        ✗ Avoid When:
          • Need instant resource availability
          • Workload is extremely predictable
          • Scaling overhead is unacceptable
          • Very short-running jobs (<1 minute)
        
        📊 Example Use Cases:
          • Interactive analytics
          • Variable batch processing
          • Development environments
          • Multi-priority job queues
        
        ⚙️ Configuration Tips:
          • Set min executors to handle baseline load
          • Set max executors to prevent runaway costs
          • Tune idle timeout based on job patterns
          • Enable shuffle service for stability
        
        
        3. ELASTIC RESOURCE POOL
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ✓ Use When:
          • Need rapid scale-up for burst workloads
          • Cost optimization is critical
          • Workload has unpredictable spikes
          • Processing real-time or streaming data
        
        ✗ Avoid When:
          • Need guaranteed resource availability
          • Cannot tolerate scaling delays
          • Workload is steady-state
          • Budget is not a concern
        
        📊 Example Use Cases:
          • Real-time analytics
          • Event-driven processing
          • Machine learning inference at scale
          • Seasonal workload patterns
        
        ⚙️ Configuration Tips:
          • Use aggressive policy for real-time workloads
          • Use conservative policy for cost savings
          • Set base executors to minimum viable
          • Configure burst capacity for peak loads
        
        
        4. HIERARCHICAL RESOURCE POOL
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ✓ Use When:
          • Multiple teams/departments share cluster
          • Need priority-based resource allocation
          • Organizational structure mirrors pools
          • Require guaranteed minimum resources
        
        ✗ Avoid When:
          • Single team or simple use case
          • No priority requirements
          • Overhead of hierarchy is too complex
          • Resource sharing is not needed
        
        📊 Example Use Cases:
          • Enterprise data platforms
          • Multi-department analytics
          • Shared research clusters
          • Production vs development isolation
        
        ⚙️ Configuration Tips:
          • Mirror organizational structure
          • Set guaranteed minimums for critical pools
          • Use weight-based fair sharing
          • Implement quota enforcement
        
        
        5. MULTI-TENANT RESOURCE POOL
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        ✓ Use When:
          • Running SaaS platform
          • Multiple external customers
          • Need strict resource isolation
          • Require billing/chargeback per tenant
        
        ✗ Avoid When:
          • Single organization/customer
          • Security isolation not required
          • Complexity overhead is too high
          • Tenant count is very small (<3)
        
        📊 Example Use Cases:
          • Data analytics SaaS
          • Multi-customer ETL platform
          • Cloud data warehouse service
          • Managed Spark service
        
        ⚙️ Configuration Tips:
          • Enable resource isolation features
          • Set per-tenant quotas and limits
          • Implement usage tracking/billing
          • Use priority weights for fair sharing
          • Monitor tenant resource usage
        
        
        HYBRID APPROACHES
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        You can combine patterns for complex scenarios:
        
        • Hierarchical + Dynamic: Different teams with auto-scaling
        • Multi-Tenant + Elastic: SaaS with burst capacity per tenant
        • Hierarchical + Multi-Tenant: Organizational + customer isolation
        
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        """
        return guide
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_performance_tuning_tips() -> str:
        """
        Performance tuning tips for resource pools.
        
        Returns:
            Formatted tips text
        """
        tips = """
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        PERFORMANCE TUNING TIPS
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        
        EXECUTOR SIZING
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        • Cores per executor: 4-6 cores (sweet spot for most workloads)
        • Memory per executor: 8-16GB (depends on data size)
        • Avoid tiny executors (<2 cores) - overhead dominates
        • Avoid huge executors (>8 cores) - GC issues
        
        Formula: 
          Executor Memory = (Dataset Size / Executors) * 2-3x buffer
        
        
        DYNAMIC ALLOCATION TUNING
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        • executorIdleTimeout: 60s (default) - adjust based on job gaps
        • cachedExecutorIdleTimeout: 300s - keep longer for cached data
        • schedulerBacklogTimeout: 1s - how long to wait before scaling up
        • sustainedSchedulerBacklogTimeout: 1s - sustained backlog trigger
        
        For Interactive Workloads:
          - Lower idle timeout (30s) for faster scale-down
          - Lower backlog timeout (1s) for faster scale-up
        
        For Batch Workloads:
          - Higher idle timeout (120s) to avoid thrashing
          - Keep default backlog timeout
        
        
        SHUFFLE OPTIMIZATION
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        • Enable external shuffle service (required for dynamic allocation)
        • Set shuffle partitions: 2-3x number of cores
        • Use appropriate shuffle partition size (128-200MB per partition)
        
        Formula:
          spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = Total Cores * 2
        
        
        MEMORY MANAGEMENT
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        • spark.memory.fraction: 0.6 (default) - execution + storage
        • spark.memory.storageFraction: 0.5 (default) - cache vs execution
        • Leave 20-30% for overhead (spark.executor.memoryOverhead)
        
        For Cache-Heavy Workloads:
          - Increase storageFraction to 0.7
        
        For Computation-Heavy Workloads:
          - Decrease storageFraction to 0.3
        
        
        PARALLELISM OPTIMIZATION
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        • Default parallelism: 2-3x total cores
        • Partition size: 128MB-256MB ideal
        • Avoid too many small partitions (overhead)
        • Avoid too few large partitions (skew)
        
        Check partition count:
          df.rdd.getNumPartitions()
        
        Repartition if needed:
          df.repartition(optimal_partitions)
        
        
        MONITORING METRICS
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Key Metrics to Watch:
        
        • Executor Utilization: Target 70-85%
        • Task Duration: Should be 100ms-5min
        • Shuffle Read/Write: Minimize if possible
        • GC Time: Should be <10% of task time
        • Data Skew: Max/Min task time ratio <3:1
        
        
        COST OPTIMIZATION
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        • Use spot/preemptible instances for non-critical workloads
        • Enable aggressive scaling for elastic pools
        • Set appropriate idle timeouts to release resources
        • Use smaller executors for better bin-packing
        • Schedule batch jobs during off-peak hours
        
        Cost Formula:
          Cost = (Executors * Hours * Rate) + Storage
        
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        """
        return tips
    
    @staticmethod
    def get_troubleshooting_guide() -> str:
        """
        Troubleshooting guide for common issues.
        
        Returns:
            Formatted troubleshooting guide
        """
        guide = """
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        
        PROBLEM: Executors Not Scaling Up
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Symptoms:
          • Jobs are slow but executor count stays low
          • Tasks are queued but no new executors added
        
        Solutions:
          ✓ Check if dynamic allocation is enabled
          ✓ Verify shuffle service is running
          ✓ Check max executors limit
          ✓ Review schedulerBacklogTimeout setting
          ✓ Ensure cluster has available capacity
        
        Debug Commands:
          spark.conf.get("spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled")
          spark.conf.get("spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors")
        
        
        PROBLEM: Executors Not Scaling Down
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Symptoms:
          • Executors remain allocated after job completion
          • High costs due to idle executors
        
        Solutions:
          ✓ Check executorIdleTimeout setting
          ✓ Unpersist cached DataFrames
          ✓ Verify no jobs are holding executors
          ✓ Review cachedExecutorIdleTimeout
        
        Debug Commands:
          spark.catalog.clearCache()
          df.unpersist()
        
        
        PROBLEM: Out of Memory Errors
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Symptoms:
          • java.lang.OutOfMemoryError
          • Tasks failing with memory errors
        
        Solutions:
          ✓ Increase executor memory
          ✓ Increase number of partitions
          ✓ Reduce partition size
          ✓ Avoid collect() on large datasets
          ✓ Use persist() strategically
          ✓ Increase memoryOverhead
        
        Quick Fixes:
          df.repartition(more_partitions)
          spark.conf.set("spark.executor.memory", "16g")
        
        
        PROBLEM: Resource Quota Exceeded
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Symptoms:
          • Jobs rejected due to quota limits
          • Tenant hitting concurrent job limits
        
        Solutions:
          ✓ Review and adjust quotas
          ✓ Implement job queuing
          ✓ Prioritize critical jobs
          ✓ Clean up completed jobs
          ✓ Request quota increase
        
        
        PROBLEM: Poor Performance Despite Resources
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Symptoms:
          • Many executors but slow jobs
          • Low CPU utilization
        
        Solutions:
          ✓ Check for data skew
          ✓ Increase parallelism
          ✓ Optimize shuffle operations
          ✓ Review query plan (explain())
          ✓ Check for small files
        
        Debug Commands:
          df.explain()
          df.rdd.glom().map(len).collect()  # Check partition sizes
        
        
        PROBLEM: Executor Lost/Failed
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Symptoms:
          • Executors being removed unexpectedly
          • Tasks restarted frequently
        
        Solutions:
          ✓ Check executor logs for errors
          ✓ Increase executor memory
          ✓ Review GC settings
          ✓ Check network connectivity
          ✓ Verify node health
        
        
        PROBLEM: Unfair Resource Distribution
        ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
        Symptoms:
          • Some pools/tenants getting more resources
          • Priority not being respected
        
        Solutions:
          ✓ Verify fair scheduler configuration
          ✓ Check pool weights
          ✓ Review priority settings
          ✓ Ensure pools are properly configured
          ✓ Check for resource leaks
        
        ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
        """
        return guide

if __name__ == "__main__":

    for tenant_id, quota in tenants_config.items():

        max_cores=480,
        max_memory_gb=1920
    )
    
    finance_hierarchy = HierarchicalResourcePool(finance_root_quota)
    
    # Create departmental pools
    finance_hierarchy.create_pool(
        "risk_management",
        PoolQuota(max_executors=50, max_cores=200, max_memory_gb=800, guaranteed_executors=20),
        PoolPriority.CRITICAL,
        "root"
    )
    
    finance_hierarchy.create_pool(
        "regulatory_reporting",
        PoolQuota(max_executors=40, max_cores=160, max_memory_gb=640, guaranteed_executors=15),
        PoolPriority.CRITICAL,
        "root"
    )
    
    finance_hierarchy.create_pool(
        "financial_analytics",
        PoolQuota(max_executors=30, max_cores=120, max_memory_gb=480, guaranteed_executors=10),
        PoolPriority.HIGH,
        "root"
    )

    print("\n  Hierarchy Structure:")
    print(finance_hierarchy.get_pool_hierarchy())

    monitor = ResourcePoolMonitor(collection_interval=10)
    
    # Setup alert handlers
    alert_log = []
    
    def email_alert_handler(alert):
        """Simulate email alert."""
        alert_log.append(alert)
        print(f"  📧 EMAIL ALERT: {alert['type']} - {alert['message']}")
    
    def slack_alert_handler(alert):
        """Simulate Slack notification."""
        print(f"  💬 SLACK: Alert in #{alert['pool_name']}: {alert['message']}")
    
    def pagerduty_handler(alert):
        """Simulate PagerDuty incident."""
        if alert['type'] == 'HIGH_UTILIZATION':
            print(f"  🚨 PAGERDUTY: Critical incident created for {alert['pool_name']}")
    
    monitor.register_alert_handler(email_alert_handler)
    monitor.register_alert_handler(slack_alert_handler)
    monitor.register_alert_handler(pagerduty_handler)
    
    # Start monitoring multi-tenant pool
    monitor.start_monitoring(mt_pool, "production_multi_tenant")
    print("  ✓ Monitoring started")
    
    # ========================================================================
    # Step 4: Execute Production Workloads
    # ========================================================================
    print("\n[4/6] Executing Production Workloads...")
    
    spark = mt_pool.spark
    
    # Define workload functions
    def finance_risk_calculation():
        """Risk management calculation job."""
        print("    → Running risk calculation...")
        df = spark.range(5000000).select(
            col("id").alias("transaction_id"),
            (rand() * 1000000).alias("amount"),
            (rand() * 100).cast("int").alias("risk_score"),
            current_timestamp().alias("calc_time")
        )
        
        risk_summary = df.groupBy(
            when(col("risk_score") < 30, "Low")
            .when(col("risk_score") < 70, "Medium")
            .otherwise("High").alias("risk_category")
        ).agg(
            count("*").alias("transaction_count"),
            sum("amount").alias("total_exposure"),
            avg("risk_score").alias("avg_risk_score")
        )
        
        return risk_summary.count()
    
    def marketing_campaign_analysis():
        """Marketing campaign analysis job."""
        print("    → Running campaign analysis...")
        df = spark.range(3000000).select(
            col("id").alias("customer_id"),
            (rand() * 10).cast("int").alias("campaign_id"),
            (rand() * 2).cast("int").alias("converted"),
            (rand() * 500).alias("revenue"),
            current_date().alias("date")
        )
        
        campaign_performance = df.groupBy("campaign_id").agg(
            count("*").alias("impressions"),
            sum("converted").alias("conversions"),
            sum("revenue").alias("total_revenue"),
            (sum("converted") / count("*") * 100).alias("conversion_rate")
        )
        
        return campaign_performance.count()
    
    def data_science_model_training():
        """ML model training job."""
        print("    → Running model training...")
        df = spark.range(8000000).select(
            col("id"),
            (rand() * 100).alias("feature1"),
            (rand() * 100).alias("feature2"),
            (rand() * 100).alias("feature3"),
            (rand() * 2).cast("int").alias("label")
        )
        
        # Feature engineering
        features = df.withColumn(
            "feature_sum", col("feature1") + col("feature2") + col("feature3")
        ).withColumn(
            "feature_product", col("feature1") * col("feature2")
        )
        
        # Aggregate statistics for training
        stats = features.groupBy("label").agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            avg("feature_sum").alias("avg_sum"),
            stddev("feature_product").alias("stddev_product")
        )
        
        return stats.count()
    
    def dev_sandbox_experiment():
        """Development sandbox experiment."""
        print("    → Running dev experiment...")
        df = spark.range(500000).select(
            col("id"),
            (rand() * 50).alias("value")
        )
        
        result = df.groupBy((col("id") % 10).alias("bucket")).agg(
            count("*").alias("count"),
            avg("value").alias("avg_value")
        )
        
        return result.count()

## README Documentation

```python
"""
Generate README.md documentation for the resource pool patterns.
"""

def generate_readme():
    """Generate comprehensive README documentation."""
    
    readme_content = """
# PySpark Resource Pool Patterns

A comprehensive implementation of resource pool patterns for Apache Spark, providing flexible and efficient resource management strategies for various workload types.

## 📋 Table of Contents

- [Overview](#overview)
- [Patterns Implemented](#patterns-implemented)
- [Installation](#installation)
- [Quick Start](#quick-start)
- [Pattern Descriptions](#pattern-descriptions)
- [Usage Examples](#usage-examples)
- [Best Practices](#best-practices)
- [Performance Tuning](#performance-tuning)
- [Monitoring](#monitoring)
- [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting)
- [API Reference](#api-reference)

## 🎯 Overview

This project implements five core resource pool patterns for PySpark, each optimized for different use cases:

1. **Static Resource Pool** - Fixed resource allocation
2. **Dynamic Resource Pool** - Automatic scaling based on demand
3. **Elastic Resource Pool** - Aggressive scaling with burst capacity
4. **Hierarchical Resource Pool** - Multi-level pools with priorities
5. **Multi-Tenant Resource Pool** - Isolated pools for multiple tenants

## 🏗️ Patterns Implemented

### 1. Static Resource Pool Pattern

**Use Case**: Predictable batch workloads with known resource requirements

**Features**:
- Fixed executor count
- Predictable costs
- Simple configuration
- Ideal for scheduled jobs

**Example**:
```python
from resource_pools import StaticResourcePool

config = {
    "executor_instances": 10,
    "executor_cores": 4,
    "executor_memory": "8g"
}

pool = StaticResourcePool(config)
pool.process_batch_job("input_path", "output_path")
pool.shutdown()
```

### 2. Dynamic Resource Pool Pattern

**Use Case**: Variable workloads with changing resource needs

**Features**:
- Automatic scaling
- Min/max executor bounds
- Idle timeout configuration
- Cost-performance balance

**Example**:
```python
from resource_pools import DynamicResourcePool

pool = DynamicResourcePool(
    min_executors=2,
    max_executors=50,
    initial_executors=5
)

pool.process_adaptive_workload(input_paths, output_base)
pool.shutdown()
```

### 3. Elastic Resource Pool Pattern

**Use Case**: Burst workloads with unpredictable spikes

**Features**:
- Rapid scale-up/down
- Multiple scaling policies
- Burst capacity support
- Cost optimization

**Example**:
```python
from resource_pools import ElasticResourcePool, ScalingPolicy

pool = ElasticResourcePool(
    base_executors=3,
    max_executors=100,
    scaling_policy=ScalingPolicy.AGGRESSIVE
)

pool.process_with_burst_capacity(
    "input_path",
    "output_path",
    complexity_factor=2.0
)
pool.shutdown()
```

### 4. Hierarchical Resource Pool Pattern

**Use Case**: Multi-team/department resource sharing

**Features**:
- Parent-child pool relationships
- Priority-based allocation
- Guaranteed minimums
- Fair sharing

**Example**:
```python
from resource_pools import HierarchicalResourcePool, PoolQuota, PoolPriority

root_quota = PoolQuota(
    max_executors=100,
    max_cores=400,
    max_memory_gb=800
)

pool = HierarchicalResourcePool(root_quota)

pool.create_pool(
    "production",
    PoolQuota(max_executors=60, guaranteed_executors=20),
    PoolPriority.CRITICAL,
    "root"
)

pool.submit_job("production", job_function, executors_needed=10)
pool.shutdown()
```

### 5. Multi-Tenant Resource Pool Pattern

**Use Case**: SaaS platforms with multiple customers

**Features**:
- Tenant isolation
- Per-tenant quotas
- Usage tracking
- Fair resource sharing

**Example**:
```python
from resource_pools import MultiTenantResourcePool, TenantQuota

pool = MultiTenantResourcePool(total_executors=100)

pool.register_tenant(
    "tenant_a",
    "Customer A",
    TenantQuota(
        max_executors=50,
        max_concurrent_jobs=10,
        priority_weight=2.0
    )
)

pool.submit_tenant_job("tenant_a", "job_name", job_function)
pool.shutdown()
```

## 🚀 Quick Start

### Installation

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/yourusername/pyspark-resource-pools.git
cd pyspark-resource-pools

# Install dependencies
pip install pyspark pandas matplotlib

# Verify installation
python resource_pools.py --help
```

### Basic Usage

```python
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from resource_pools import DynamicResourcePool

# Create pool
pool = DynamicResourcePool(min_executors=2, max_executors=20)

# Get Spark session
spark = pool.spark

# Process data
df = spark.read.parquet("input_data")
result = df.groupBy("category").count()
result.write.parquet("output_data")

# Cleanup
pool.shutdown()
```

## 📚 Pattern Descriptions

### When to Use Each Pattern

| Pattern | Workload Type | Scaling | Cost | Complexity |
|---------|--------------|---------|------|------------|
| Static | Predictable batch | None | Fixed | Low |
| Dynamic | Variable batch | Automatic | Variable | Medium |
| Elastic | Burst/Spike | Aggressive | Optimized | Medium |
| Hierarchical | Multi-team | Priority-based | Shared | High |
| Multi-Tenant | SaaS/Multi-customer | Per-tenant | Isolated | High |

### Pattern Selection Decision Tree

```
Is workload predictable?
├─ Yes → Static Pool
└─ No
   ├─ Single organization?
   │  ├─ Yes → Dynamic or Elastic Pool
   │  └─ No → Multi-Tenant Pool
   └─ Multiple teams/priorities?
      └─ Yes → Hierarchical Pool
```

## 💡 Best Practices

### Executor Sizing

```python
# Good: Balanced executor size
config = {
    "executor_cores": 4,
    "executor_memory": "12g"
}

# Avoid: Too small (overhead dominates)
config = {
    "executor_cores": 1,
    "executor_memory": "2g"
}

# Avoid: Too large (GC issues)
config = {
    "executor_cores": 16,
    "executor_memory": "64g"
}
```

### Dynamic Allocation Tuning

```python
# Interactive workloads
pool = DynamicResourcePool(
    min_executors=2,
    max_executors=30,
    initial_executors=5
)
spark.conf.set("spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout", "30s")

# Batch workloads
pool = DynamicResourcePool(
    min_executors=5,
    max_executors=100,
    initial_executors=20
)
spark.conf.set("spark.dynamicAllocation.executorIdleTimeout", "120s")
```

### Memory Configuration

```python
# Calculate executor memory
dataset_size_gb = 100
num_executors = 20
executor_memory_gb = (dataset_size_gb / num_executors) * 3  # 3x buffer

config = {
    "executor_memory": f"{int(executor_memory_gb)}g",
    "spark.executor.memoryOverhead": f"{int(executor_memory_gb * 0.1)}g"
}
```

## 📊 Monitoring

### Enable Monitoring

```python
from resource_pools import ResourcePoolMonitor

monitor = ResourcePoolMonitor(collection_interval=60)

# Register alert handler
def alert_handler(alert):
    print(f"Alert: {alert['message']}")

monitor.register_alert_handler(alert_handler)

# Start monitoring
monitor.start_monitoring(pool, "my_pool")

# Get metrics
summary = monitor.get_metrics_summary(last_n_minutes=60)
print(summary)

# Export metrics
monitor.export_metrics("metrics.json", format='json')
monitor.stop_monitoring()
```

### Key Metrics to Monitor

- **Executor Utilization**: Target 70-85%
- **Task Duration**: Should be 100ms-5min
- **Shuffle Size**: Minimize if possible
- **GC Time**: Should be <10% of task time
- **Data Skew**: Max/Min ratio <3:1

## 🔧 Troubleshooting

### Common Issues

**Problem**: Executors not scaling up
```python
# Check configuration
spark.conf.get("spark.dynamicAllocation.enabled")  # Should be "true"
spark.conf.get("spark.shuffle.service.enabled")     # Should be "true"

# Verify max executors
spark.conf.get("spark.dynamicAllocation.maxExecutors")
```

**Problem**: Out of memory errors
```python
# Increase partitions
df = df.repartition(200)

# Increase executor memory
spark.conf.set("spark.executor.memory", "16g")

# Check partition sizes
df.rdd.glom().map(len).collect()
```

**Problem**: Slow performance despite resources
```python
# Check for data skew
df.groupBy("key").count().orderBy(desc("count")).show()

# Optimize shuffle partitions
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", total_cores * 2)

# Review query plan
df.explain()
```

## 🎓 Advanced Usage

### Combining Patterns

```python
# Multi-tenant with hierarchical structure
mt_pool = MultiTenantResourcePool(total_executors=200)

# Register tenant
mt_pool.register_tenant(
    "enterprise",
    "Enterprise Customer",
    TenantQuota(max_executors=100, max_concurrent_jobs=20, priority_weight=3.0)
)

# Create hierarchical pools for tenant
h_pool = HierarchicalResourcePool(PoolQuota(max_executors=100))
h_pool.create_pool("critical", PoolQuota(max_executors=60), PoolPriority.CRITICAL, "root")
h_pool.create_pool("normal", PoolQuota(max_executors=40), PoolPriority.MEDIUM, "root")

# Submit jobs through both layers
mt_pool.submit_tenant_job("enterprise", "job1", job_func)
h_pool.submit_job("critical", job_func, executors_needed=20)
```

### Custom Scaling Policies

```python
class CustomElasticPool(ElasticResourcePool):
    def _calculate_required_executors(self, data_size_gb: float, complexity_factor: float) -> int:
        # Custom logic for executor calculation
        if data_size_gb > 100:
            return min(int(data_size_gb / 1.5), self.max_executors)
        else:
            return min(int(data_size_gb / 2), self.max_executors)

pool = CustomElasticPool(base_executors=5, max_executors=100)
```

### Custom Monitoring

```python
class CustomMonitor(ResourcePoolMonitor):
    def _check_anomalies(self, snapshot: MetricSnapshot):
        super()._check_anomalies(snapshot)
        
        # Custom anomaly detection
        if snapshot.executors_active > 80:
            self._trigger_alert(
                "VERY_HIGH_USAGE",
                f"Executor count exceeds 80: {snapshot.executors_active}",
                snapshot
            )

monitor = CustomMonitor(collection_interval=30)

# PySpark Data Migration Strategy Patterns
